metadata.title: EAU Guidelines on Sexual and Reproductive Health
metadata.summary: The document reviews the epidemiology of male sexual dysfunction and ejaculatory disorders. It addresses the causes, diagnostic evaluation, cardiovascular risk assessment, treatment and follow-up of erectile dysfunction, including erectile dysfunction after prostate cancer treatment. Treatment options range from counselling and medication to devices, investigational approaches and surgery.

target_population: men with ED and known CVD
men with ED after radical prostatectomy or other prostate cancer treatment
young patients with pelvic or perineal trauma
men who have sex with men
therapeutic_areas: lifestyle changes and risk factor modification

toxicities.incidence: Sildenafil: 1.2%; Tadalafil: 2.3%; Vardenafil: 2%; Avanafil, 200mg: 0.6%. With intra-urethral alprostadil, dizziness with possible hypotension: 1.9-14%.
Sildenafil: 1.9%; Vardenafil: < 2%. The table reports None for Avanafil, 200mg.
Dizziness with possible hypotension during intra-urethral alprostadil treatment: 1.9-14%. No incidence is given for the other specified combinations or for intracavernous treatment.
recognition: Blood-pressure reduction and symptoms of hypotension with concomitant PDE5Is and organic nitrates or NO donors
Usually minor additional blood-pressure reduction when PDE5Is are given with antihypertensive agents
Mild systemic hypotension with intracavernous alprostadil, particularly at higher doses
prevention: Do not use PDE5Is together with any organic nitrate or NO donor, including recreational amyl nitrite or nitrate (poppers); concomitant use is absolutely contraindicated.
Do not use PDE5Is concurrently with nicorandil.
Consider the potential combined blood-pressure effects of PDE5Is and α-blockers; the guide states that their simultaneous use is not currently restricted.

toxicities.event: Local penile pain, burning and erythema
toxicities.incidence: Local pain with intra-urethral alprostadil: 29-41%. With intracavernous alprostadil, 50% of patients reported pain after only 11% of total injections. No incidence is specified for pain with the other listed treatments.
recognition: Penile erythema, burning or pain after topical alprostadil; these effects usually resolve within two hours of application
Pain during vacuum erection device use

management.actions: Pain generally subsides with continued use; adding sodium bicarbonate or using local anaesthesia may relieve it.

prevention: Using lower doses of the component drugs in intracavernous combinations can lessen adverse effects; Trimix has a lower incidence of penile pain than alprostadil monotherapy because it contains a lower alprostadil dose.

toxicities.incidence: Intra-urethral alprostadil: priapism < 1%. Intracavernous alprostadil: unwanted, excessively prolonged erections 5% and priapism 1%. The guide describes a virtually negligible risk of priapism with InvicorpTM without giving a percentage.
prevention: Intracavernous alprostadil is contraindicated in men at risk of priapism.

toxicities.incidence: Intra-urethral alprostadil: penile fibrosis < 1%. Intracavernous alprostadil: fibrosis 2%. When papaverine is used, fibrosis occurs in 5-10%, depending on total dose.
recognition: Tunical fibrosis, which may indicate early Peyronie’s disease

management.actions: Temporarily stop the injection programme; cavernosal fibrosis usually resolves within a few months.
Consider stopping intracavernous injections indefinitely because this finding may indicate early Peyronie’s disease.

toxicities.dose_modifications: Temporary interruption of intracavernous injections is described for cavernosal fibrosis; tunical fibrosis may warrant indefinite discontinuation.

toxicities.incidence: 5%; the guide attributes this event to the administration route.

toxicities.event: Adverse effects of vacuum erection devices
prevention: Vacuum erection devices are contraindicated in patients with bleeding disorders or receiving anticoagulant therapy.

toxicities.event: Skin necrosis associated with a constriction ring
prevention: Remove the constriction ring within 30 minutes to avoid this serious adverse event.

toxicities.event: Mechanical failure of a penile prosthesis
toxicities.incidence: Technical changes to commonly used three-piece prostheses resulted in mechanical failure rates of < 5% after 5 years of follow-up. A meta-analysis reported implant durability or survival of 93.3% at 1 year, 91.0% at 3 years, 87.2% at 5 years, 76.8% at 10 years, 63.7% at 15 years, and 52.9% at 20 years.

With primary implantation in low-risk patients at high-volume centres using careful surgery and appropriate antibiotic prophylaxis: 2-3%. With an antibiotic-impregnated or hydrophilic-coated prosthesis, the rate may decrease to 1-2%. Published series of patients with spinal cord injury reported infection in up to 16% of cases.

management.actions: Remove the device and administer antibiotics. Immediate replacement after removal and wash-out is an alternative described with successful salvage in > 80% of cases; the guide gives no absolute recommendation between approaches and calls for discussion of salvage benefits and harms with the patient.

prevention: Use appropriate perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis against Gram-positive and negative bacteria and meticulous surgical technique.
Coated prostheses and techniques that limit wound exposure and skin contact, including the no-touch technique, appear to lower infection rates.
Identify and treat nasal Staphylococcus aureus colonisation before surgery: an RCT reported a reduction in postoperative surgical-site infection from 4.4% to 0.9% with mupirocin and chlorhexidine.

In a retrospective analysis of men with diabetes receiving a Coloplast Titan™ implant, vancomycin plus gentamicin was the most effective antibiotic combination for implant dipping against postoperative infection, explantation and revision.
The guide notes that evidence is not definitive for prolonged postoperative antibiotics (> 24 hours), shaving with clippers or preparation with chlorhexidine-alcohol.

toxicities.incidence: Impending implant erosion after surgery: 1-6% of cases.
recognition: Impending erosion affecting the distal corpora, urethra or glans
Injury to the bladder, bowel or blood vessels
prevention: A two-piece inflatable prosthesis may be an option for patients at high risk of complications from reservoir placement, such as those with previous abdominal surgery.

toxicities.event: Local adverse effects after intracavernous BoNT-A
recognition: Mild local side effects were reported in both cited trials; neither trial reported systemic complications.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Use appropriate antibiotics active against Gram-positive and negative bacteria alongside careful surgical technique for penile prosthesis implantation.

prophylaxis.type: Pre-treatment of nasal Staphylococcus aureus colonisation
prophylaxis.recommendation: An RCT found that identifying patients colonised with nasal Staphylococcus aureus and treating them with mupirocin and chlorhexidine before surgery reduced postoperative surgical-site infection from 4.4% to 0.9%.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients colonised with nasal Staphylococcus aureus before surgery.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: Urinary tract infections associated with intra-urethral alprostadil

infection_management.prevention: Appropriate antibiotic prophylaxis against Gram-positive and negative bacteria, coated implants and surgical techniques that minimise wound exposure and skin contact appear to reduce infection. Preoperative treatment of nasal Staphylococcus aureus colonisation with mupirocin and chlorhexidine reduced postoperative surgical-site infection from 4.4% to 0.9% in an RCT.
infection_management.management: Remove the infected prosthesis and administer antibiotics. Immediate salvage with wash-out and replacement is another described approach, with success in > 80% of cases. The guide does not establish an absolute choice after removal; discuss the benefits and harms of salvage with the patient.

recommendations.statement: Obtain a thorough medical and sexual history from every patient presenting with erectile dysfunction (ED), including a focused psychosexual history covering life stressors, cultural factors and thoughts related to sexual performance.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.5.6 Summary of evidence and recommendations for diagnostic evaluation of ED

recommendations.statement: Use a validated ED questionnaire, such as the International Index of Erectile Function, to evaluate every domain of sexual function and the effects of a particular treatment.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.5.6 Summary of evidence and recommendations for diagnostic evaluation of ED

recommendations.statement: Perform a focused physical examination during the initial evaluation of men with ED to detect underlying medical conditions and associated genital disorders.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.5.6 Summary of evidence and recommendations for diagnostic evaluation of ED

recommendations.statement: Assess laboratory results, including glucose and lipid profiles and total testosterone, to identify and address reversible risk factors and modifiable lifestyle factors.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.5.6 Summary of evidence and recommendations for diagnostic evaluation of ED

recommendations.statement: Include specific diagnostic tests in the initial ED evaluation when the indications listed in Table 5.2 are present.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.5.6 Summary of evidence and recommendations for diagnostic evaluation of ED

recommendations.statement: Explain fully to patients how phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors (PDE5Is) work and how to take them.
recommendations.rationale: Incorrect use or insufficient information is the main cause of failure to respond to PDE5Is.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.6.12 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of ED

recommendations.statement: When indicated, refer the patient for Cognitive Behaviour Therapy that includes the partner, alongside medical treatment, to optimise treatment outcomes.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.6.12 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of ED

recommendations.statement: Discuss the risk of sexual changes beyond erectile dysfunction (ED) with patients receiving active treatment for prostate cancer, including reduced sexual desire, altered orgasm, anejaculation, Peyronie’s like disease and changes in penile size.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.6.12 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of ED

recommendations.statement: Begin lifestyle changes and modification of risk factors before starting ED treatment or concurrently with it.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.6.12 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of ED

recommendations.statement: Use PDE5Is as the first-line treatment for ED.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.6.12 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of ED

recommendations.statement: Offer intracavernous injections either as an alternative first-line treatment for well-informed patients or as second-line treatment.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.6.12 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of ED

recommendations.statement: Offer topical/intra-urethral alprostadil as an alternative first-line treatment to well-informed patients who do not want or are unsuitable for oral vasoactive treatment, who do not want intracavernous injections, or who prefer a less-invasive option.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.6.12 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of ED

recommendations.statement: Use low intensity shockwave treatment (LI-SWT), with or without PDE5Is, for patients with mild vasculogenic ED, as an alternative for well-informed patients who do not want or are unsuitable for oral vasoactive treatment, or for patients with vasculogenic ED who respond poorly to PDE5Is.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.6.12 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of ED

recommendations.statement: Use vacuum erection devices for well-informed patients seeking ED treatment that is non-invasive and does not involve drugs.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.6.12 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of ED

recommendations.statement: Use daily supplements containing L-arginine or ginseng for men with mild ED who decline pharmacological treatment, after advising them that any improvement in EF may be mild.
recommendations.context: Mild ED when pharmacological treatment is declined
recommendations.source_heading: 5.6.12 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of ED

recommendations.statement: Implant a penile prosthesis when other treatments have failed or when the patient prefers this option, after fully explaining its potential benefits and harms.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.6.12 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of ED

recommendations.statement: Advise patients that the available evidence does not adequately support a particular penile rehabilitation regimen.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.6.12 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of ED

recommendations.statement: Begin pro-erectile treatment as early as possible after radical prostatectomy/pelvic surgery or other curative treatment for prostate cancer.
recommendations.context: After radical prostatectomy/pelvic surgery or other curative treatment for prostate cancer

conditions.name: Erectile dysfunction
conditions.description: Persistent difficulty obtaining and maintaining an erection adequate for satisfactory sexual activity. Its causes may involve vascular, neurological, anatomical, hormonal, medication-related and psychological pathways, often in combination. It can adversely affect patients’ and partners’ psychosocial well-being and quality of life.
conditions.epidemiology: The MMAS reported ED in 52% of noninstitutionalised men aged 40-70 years in the Boston area: 17.2% minimal, 25.2% moderate and 9.6% complete. In the Cologne study of men aged 30-80 years, prevalence was 19.2% and increased with age from 2.3% to 53.4%. Annual incidence per 1,000 men was 26 in long-term MMAS data and 19.2 in a Dutch study with mean follow-up of 4.2 years. Among men seeking initial care for newly developed ED, one in four was younger than 40 years, and almost 50% of those younger men reported severe ED. Differences between studies may reflect their methods and populations.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Assessment addresses the rigidity and duration of stimulated and morning erections, together with desire, arousal, ejaculation and orgasm. ED may coexist with symptoms of hypogonadism or other sexual problems. Its reported risk factors include age, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia, hypertension, CVD, obesity, MetS, inactivity, smoking and drug use, among other medical and psychological conditions.

subtypes.name: organic
subtypes.distinguishing_features: An aetiological category; the guide cautions that many presentations have both organic and psychological contributors.

subtypes.name: psychogenic
subtypes.distinguishing_features: An aetiological category that may involve generalised or situational psychological factors.

subtypes.name: mixed ED
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Organic and psychological contributors coexist; the guide describes this as the situation in most cases.

subtypes.name: primary organic
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A suggested designation when organic factors predominate.

subtypes.name: primary psychogenic
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A suggested designation when psychological factors predominate.

diagnostic_workup.test: Nocturnal penile tumescence and rigidity (NPTR) test
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure nocturnal erectile episodes, tumescence, maximum rigidity and duration to help distinguish organic from psychogenic ED.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Selected patients requiring specific diagnostic assessment; perform on at least two separate nights.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An erectile event with tip rigidity of at least 60% lasting ≥ 10 minutes indicates a functional erectile mechanism. Psychogenic ED usually produces normal findings. Several confounding factors and uncertainty about correspondence with sexual erections limit routine diagnostic use.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess erectile response, although it provides limited information about vascular status.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Selected patients requiring specific diagnostic assessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A rigid erection that cannot be bent, begins within 10 minutes and lasts for 30 minutes is positive. The test alone is diagnostically inconclusive; request penile duplex Doppler assessment when clinically warranted.

diagnostic_workup.test: Dynamic duplex ultrasound (US) of the penis
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate the haemodynamic basis of erectile function.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Usually when vasculogenic ED is suspected, including with diabetes mellitus, multiple CV risk factors, overt peripheral vascular disease, renal transplantation or poor response to oral therapy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Peak systolic blood flow > 30 cm/s, end-diastolic velocity < 3 cm/s and resistance index > 0.8 are considered normal; a normal examination makes further vascular investigation unnecessary. Anxiety or insufficient vasoactive-agent dosage can contribute to false-positive findings.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Only when penile revascularisation is under consideration.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess suspected venogenic dysfunction.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Infrequently used for venogenic ED; also used to exclude corporeal veno-occlusive dysfunction before post-traumatic revascularisation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guide notes that the concept of venogenic ED has been questioned.

prognostic_tools.name: Erectile Hardness Score (EHS)
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Supported as a measure of erectile rigidity; the guide provides no score thresholds.

prognostic_tools.name: IIEF
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Used to assess sexual-function domains and treatment effects; the guide provides no score-based categories.

follow_up.survivorship_notes: Treatment success should be judged beyond efficacy and safety, and management should account for differences between patients and situations.

conditions.name: vasculogenic ED
conditions.description: ED with a suspected or established vascular mechanism; this mechanism is particularly relevant to cardiovascular risk assessment and penile haemodynamic testing.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Potential vascular contributors include cardiovascular disease, hypertension, peripheral vasculopathy, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidaemia, metabolic syndrome, hyperhomocysteinemia, smoking, inactivity and obesity. ED may precede recognised CVD; greater severity and longer duration are associated with greater cardiovascular risk.

diagnostic_workup.test: 2019 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association atherosclerotic CVD (ASCVD) risk score
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Estimate the probability of a major CV event over the next 10 years.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: The Princeton Consensus Conference IV recommends it for all men evaluated for predominantly vasculogenic ED.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Categories are low risk < 5%; borderline risk 5% to < 7.5%; intermediate risk ≥ 7.5% to < 20%; and high risk ≥ 20%.

diagnostic_workup.test: Non-contrast-enhanced cardiac computed tomography for coronary artery calcium (CAC) scores
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess subclinical CAD and refine cardiovascular risk.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: The Princeton Conference IV Expert Panel recommended it for men in the borderline to intermediate ASCVD risk category, particularly because risk may be underestimated in men aged 40 to 60 years.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The proposed flowchart distinguishes CAC = O, CAC 1 to 100 and CAC > 100. Use of the flowcharts should account for local expertise, test availability, cost effectiveness and individual clinical profiles.

diagnostic_workup.test: Dynamic duplex ultrasound (US) of the penis
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterise penile haemodynamics and potentially inform ED treatment selection.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Suspected vascular aetiology, including diabetes mellitus, multiple CV risk factors, overt peripheral vascular disease, renal transplantation or poor response to oral treatment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Normal values are peak systolic blood flow > 30 cm/s, end-diastolic velocity < 3 cm/s and resistance index > 0.8. A normal result obviates additional vascular investigation; diagnostic accuracy may be affected by confounding factors.

prognostic_tools.name: ASCVD

risk_groups.criteria: 5% to < 7.5% risk over the next 10 years
≥ 7.5% to < 20% risk over the next 10 years

prognostic_tools.interpretation: Uses the Pooled Cohort Equations (PCE) to estimate major CV event risk; when used alone, it may substantially underestimate risk in men aged 40 to 60 years.

prognostic_tools.name: CAC
components: Coronary artery calcium measured with non-contrast-enhanced cardiac computed tomography
prognostic_tools.interpretation: The Princeton Consensus Conference IV identifies CAC scoring as a particularly strong predictor for guiding CVD risk assessment.

recommended_tests: Assess ED treatment efficacy and safety

conditions.name: psychogenic ED
conditions.description: ED in which psychological contributors predominate; the guide cautions against assuming a purely psychological cause because mixed aetiology is common.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Potential contributors include depression, anxiety, transient distress, relationship dissatisfaction, emotional disconnection, dysfunctional sexual expectations, poor self-esteem and distraction from erotic cues. Presentations may be generalised or situational.

subtypes.name: Generalised type
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Examples include reduced capacity for arousal or difficulty with sexual intimacy.

subtypes.name: Situational type
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Examples involve a partner, performance concerns or distress.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Examine life stressors, psychological symptoms, relationship and intimacy factors, cultural background, sexual expectations and cognitive patterns.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Psychosexual assessment of ED; tailor evaluation to the context of sexual minorities.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the psychosocial context of erectile difficulties.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Psychosocial assessment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help distinguish psychological from organic erectile difficulties.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Selected cases requiring specific diagnostic tests.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Findings are usually normal in psychogenic ED, although confounding factors limit routine diagnostic use.

conditions.name: ED after RP
conditions.description: Erectile difficulty following radical prostatectomy. Damage to neurovascular structures during pelvic surgery may contribute, even though nerve-sparing approaches are used.
conditions.epidemiology: Studies cited by the guide report post-RP ED in 25-75% of men, while unassisted recovery of post-operative erectile function ranges between 20 and 25% in most studies. In the ProtecT trial, erections firm enough for intercourse were reported by 67% at baseline and, at six-year follow-up, by 30% in the active monitoring group, 27%% in the RT group and 17% in the RP group. Patient age, erectile function before surgery, surgical volume and preservation of neurovascular bundles influence post-operative erectile outcomes; evidence comparing surgical approaches is conflicting.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Reduced erectile function after RP may occur alongside other changes in sexual health. The guide reports that penile rehabilitation following nerve-sparing RP has not been shown to increase spontaneous erectile-function recovery.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish pre-operative function and evaluate erectile outcomes following surgery.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Assessment of patients undergoing or recovering from RP.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Age, baseline EF and the quality of nerve-sparing technique are identified as potential predictors of outcome.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure sexual function, including erectile function.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Used for sexual-function assessment in the cited ProtecT trial and a cited comparison of surgery with RT.

long_term_effects: Possible changes in sexual desire, orgasm, ejaculation, penile shape or penile size after active treatment for prostate cancer
follow_up.survivorship_notes: The guide states that evidence is insufficient to identify a particular penile-rehabilitation regimen that reliably produces spontaneous, unassisted erections.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before considering penile revascularisation.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Used infrequently for this assessment.

conditions.name: Premature ejaculation
conditions.epidemiology: The NHSLS reported an overall prevalence of 31% among men aged 18-59 years, with rates of 30% at 18-29 years, 32% at 30-39 years, 28% at 40-49 years and 55% at 50-59 years. The guide questions whether prevalence is as high as 20-30%, noting that relatively few men seek care and that a single yes/no question may inflate estimates; European studies reported significantly lower rates. Two observational cross-sectional surveys reported overall prevalences of 19.8 and 25.8%, respectively. In those studies, rates were 2.3 and 3.18% for lifelong PE, 3.9 and 4.48% for acquired PE, 8.5 and 11.38% for variable PE, and 5.1 and 6.4% for subjective PE, respectively. Men with acquired PE sought treatment more often than men with lifelong PE in both surveys.
conditions.clinical_presentation: A complaint that ejaculation takes place too early; reported prevalence depends substantially on how that complaint is assessed.

subtypes.name: lifelong PE
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A classification identified in the cited surveys; reported rates were 2.3 and 3.18%, respectively.

subtypes.name: acquired PE
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A classification identified in the cited surveys; reported rates were 3.9 and 4.48%, respectively, and affected men were more likely to seek treatment than men with lifelong PE.

subtypes.name: variable PE
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A classification identified in the cited surveys; reported rates were 8.5 and 11.38%, respectively.

subtypes.name: subjective PE
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A classification identified in the cited surveys; reported rates were 5.1 and 6.4%, respectively.

conditions.name: Delayed ejaculation
conditions.description: An ejaculatory disorder whose epidemiological assessment is complicated by uncertain definitions.
conditions.epidemiology: Several epidemiological studies estimated prevalence at around 3% among sexually active men. In the NHSLS, 7.78% of a national sample of 1,246 men aged 18-59 years reported inability to climax or ejaculate. A British survey reported inability to reach orgasm in 0.7% of men, while an international survey found that 1.1-2.8% of men frequently experienced that difficulty. In a USA sample of men aged 57-85 years, 20% reported inability to climax and 73% reported being troubled by it. Although evidence is limited, estimated prevalences of lifelong and acquired DE are 1 and 4%, respectively.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Difficulty reaching climax or ejaculating; the guide distinguishes lifelong, acquired and situational presentations.

subtypes.name: lifelong DE
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Estimated prevalence of 1%, based on limited evidence.

subtypes.name: acquired DE
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Estimated prevalence of 4%, based on limited evidence.

subtypes.name: situational DE
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Identified as a distinct presentation; no separate prevalence is supplied.

conditions.name: Anejaculation
conditions.description: Inability to ejaculate; estimates are difficult because the condition is uncommon and some men cannot distinguish ejaculation from orgasm.
conditions.epidemiology: Kinsey et al. reported anejaculation in 0.14% of the general population.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Spinal cord injury, diabetes mellitus and multiple sclerosis are described as the most common causes. In most cases involving spinal cord injury, ejaculation requires medical assistance.

conditions.name: Anorgasmia
conditions.description: Difficulty attaining orgasm; its exact prevalence is difficult to determine because it is uncommon and ejaculation and orgasm are not always distinguished by respondents.
conditions.epidemiology: A USA report found that 8% of men had unsuccessfully attempted to achieve orgasm during the past year; the report is discussed in the context of anejaculation and anorgasmia rather than as a separately established prevalence for either condition.

conditions.name: Retrograde ejaculation
conditions.description: An ejaculatory dysfunction whose true incidence is difficult to establish. The guide links it to diabetic autonomic neuropathy and to disruption of bladder-neck integrity after prostate surgery.
conditions.epidemiology: RE is generally reported in 0.3-2% of patients attending fertility clinics. It was observed with a 6% incidence among 54 diabetic patients with sexual dysfunction, in 34.6% of diabetic men in a controlled trial, and in at least 8.8% of 57 patients with type-1-diabetes mellitus aged 18-50 years in another trial. In a study of 5,276 men after TURP, 68% reported post-surgical RE. The guide states that incidence after surgical treatment of LUTS decreases with less-invasive techniques.
conditions.clinical_presentation: May occur with diabetes-related autonomic neuropathy or following TURP or open prostatectomy. Depending on the extent of sympathetic autonomic neuropathy, associated ejaculatory difficulties can range from DE to RE and anejaculation.

conditions.name: Painful ejaculation
conditions.description: A poorly understood condition associated with sexual dysfunction.
conditions.epidemiology: Studies cited by the guide reported prevalence of 1-10% in the general population and 30-75% among men with chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome (CP/CPPS). The guide cautions that most study designs were not scientifically sound and that the condition may have been under-reported because evidence-based definitions and clear prognostic criteria were lacking.

conditions.name: Haemospermia
conditions.description: A symptom whose frequency is difficult to establish because it may go unnoticed, often resolves without intervention and can cause embarrassment.
conditions.epidemiology: Haemospermia accounts for 1-1.5% of urological referrals, occurs across age groups and has a reported mean age of 37 years. In a PCa screening study involving 26,126 men aged > 50 years or older than 40 with a history of PCa or of black ethnicity, 0.5% had haemospermia when entering the trial.

conditions.name: Low sexual desire
conditions.description: Reduced sexual desire in men, reported in both solitary and partnered contexts.
conditions.epidemiology: Reported global prevalence in men is 3-28%. Low solitary and dyadic sexual desires were reported in 68% and 14% of men, respectively. Reported prevalence among gay men is 19-57%; among young men aged 18-29 years, it is 6-19%. The guide notes a relationship with age without restricting the complaint to older men.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Reduced sexual desire, which may concern solitary or dyadic sexual activity.

subtypes.name: Low solitary sexual desire
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Reported in 68% of men in the cited data.

subtypes.name: Low dyadic sexual desire
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Reported in 14% of men in the cited data.

therapies_index.name: PDE5Is
approved_indications: First-line treatment of ED; treatment of ED after nerve-sparing surgery
therapies_index.administration: Oral therapy. The choice of agent depends on the anticipated frequency of intercourse and the patient's experience.
key_toxicities: Adverse effects are generally mild and self-limiting.
Concomitant organic nitrates, NO donors or nicorandil can cause unpredictable blood-pressure reductions and hypotensive symptoms.
monitoring: Check that the prescribed medicine is licensed and used correctly, including its dose, timing and the need for sexual stimulation.
Assess erectile response, adverse effects and treatment satisfaction.

therapies_index.name: sildenafil
approved_indications: ED
therapies_index.administration: Doses of 25, 50 and 100 mg; recommended initial dose 50 mg, adjusted to response and adverse effects. Its effect begins 30-60 minutes after administration and can last up to 12 hours. An orally disintegrating tablet is available in doses of 25, 50, 75 and 100 mg; an oral suspension has also been developed.
monitoring: Assess response and adverse effects when adjusting the dose.

therapies_index.name: tadalafil
approved_indications: ED
ED with LUTS
therapies_index.administration: On-demand doses of 10 and 20 mg, starting at 10 mg and adjusting to response and adverse effects; effectiveness begins at 30 minutes, peaks after approximately 2 hours and can last up to 36 hours. For once-daily use, 2.5 or 5 mg may be considered; the recommended daily dose is 5 mg at approximately the same time each day.
monitoring: Adjust on-demand dosing according to response and adverse effects.
Reassess periodically whether continued daily treatment remains appropriate.

therapies_index.name: vardenafil
approved_indications: ED
therapies_index.administration: On-demand doses of 5, 10 and 20 mg; recommended initial dose 10 mg, adjusted to response and adverse effects. It is effective from 30 minutes after administration. An orodispersable tablet is also available.
monitoring: Assess response and adverse effects when adjusting the dose.

therapies_index.name: avanafil
approved_indications: ED
therapies_index.administration: On-demand doses of 50, 100 and 200 mg; recommended initial dose 100 mg taken 15-30 minutes before sexual activity, with adjustment according to efficacy and tolerability.
monitoring: Assess efficacy and tolerability when adjusting the dose.

therapies_index.name: alprostadil
therapies_index.mechanism: The guide identifies it as a vasoactive agent.
approved_indications: Topical or intra-urethral treatment of ED
Intracavernous treatment of ED
therapies_index.administration: Topical cream delivers 200 and 300 μg through the urethral meatus. An intra-urethral pellet is generally started at 500 μg and may be increased to 1000 μg if the response is unsatisfactory. Intracavernous monotherapy uses 5-40 μg; an office-based injection-training programme is required.
key_toxicities: Topical use: penile erythema, burning and pain, usually resolving within two hours.
Intra-urethral use: local pain (29-41%), dizziness with possible hypotension (1.9-14%), rare penile fibrosis and priapism (< 1%), urethral bleeding (5%) and urinary tract infections (0.2%).
Intracavernous use: penile pain, prolonged unwanted erections, priapism, fibrosis and occasional mild systemic hypotension, particularly at higher doses.
monitoring: Provide injection-technique training and close follow-up during intracavernous treatment.
Assess for cavernosal or tunical fibrosis during intracavernous treatment.

therapies_index.name: VITAROSTM
therapies_index.mechanism: Its cream contains an absorption enhancer that facilitates delivery of alprostadil through the urethral meatus.
approved_indications: ED
therapies_index.administration: Topical alprostadil at a dose of 300 μg; available in some European countries.

therapies_index.name: MUSE™
approved_indications: ED
therapies_index.administration: Alprostadil pellet inserted intra-urethrally; treatment is generally initiated at 500 μg and can be increased to 1000 μg if the clinical response is inadequate.
monitoring: Assess the clinical response before increasing the dose.

therapies_index.name: Intracavernous injections

therapies_index.administration: Intracavernous injection of a vasoactive drug; patients can be offered this option at any stage of an individualised treatment assessment.
monitoring: Train patients in injection technique and arrange close follow-up.

therapies_index.administration: Used for intracavernous injection, most often in combinations; the text gives 20-80 mg. It is not licensed for ED and has been abandoned as monotherapy.

therapies_index.name: Phentolamine
