special_populations.population: Men with predominantly vasculogenic ED and no overt CVD or cardiac symptoms
special_populations.considerations: Cardiovascular assessment is relevant because ED may precede CVD. The Princeton Consensus Conference IV recommends calculating 10-year ASCVD risk in this population. For men in the borderline or intermediate risk categories, it also recommends CAC measurement, particularly because risk may be underestimated in men aged 40 to 60 years. Use of the proposed assessment pathways should account for local expertise, test availability, cost effectiveness and individual clinical circumstances.

special_populations.population: Men with ED and overt CV symptoms or known CVD
special_populations.considerations: The cardiovascular assessment considers the risk of an adverse event during or shortly after sexual activity. Low-risk patients can generally undertake modest exercise without symptoms. Patients at intermediate or indeterminable risk require exercise stress testing before resuming sexual activity; a chemical stress test with echocardiography or nuclear imaging is an option if a standard exercise test cannot be completed. High-risk patients have severe or unstable cardiac conditions that make sexual activity a significant risk.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: The management pathway directs high-risk patients, and intermediate-risk patients who fail stress testing, to cardiology assessment. It allows ED treatment for patients assessed as low risk.

special_populations.population: Men with ED who use nitrates or riociguat
special_populations.considerations: Concomitant PDE5Is and organic nitrates or NO donors are absolutely contraindicated because blood pressure may fall unpredictably. Concurrent nicorandil and PDE5Is are also contraindicated. The management pathway separately considers whether nitrates remain necessary in patients taking nitrates or riociguat.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: If nitrates are necessary, the pathway uses non-PDE5Is treatment for ED; it considers PDE5Is only if nitrates have been stopped.

special_populations.population: Men with ED and concomitant LUTS
special_populations.considerations: Tadalafil 5 mg is identified as licensed for both ED and LUTS. Combining PDE5Is with α-blockers calls for attention to possible cumulative blood-pressure effects, although the cited meta-analysis did not find an increased rate of adverse events due to hypotension.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Consider tadalafil 5 mg for mild to moderate LUTS associated with ED, either alone or with α-blockers.

special_populations.population: Men with ED who do not respond adequately to PDE5Is
special_populations.considerations: Assessment should first establish whether a licensed drug was prescribed and used correctly, including its dose, timing and the need for sexual stimulation. High-fat meals can delay absorption of sildenafil, vardenafil and avanafil. Evidence that switching between PDE5Is improves response has not been reported in the available RCTs.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: After correcting use and providing education, the relevant PDE5I may be tried again. For refractory or complex ED, combination treatment should be considered as a first-line approach; options described include PDE5Is with LI-SWT, a VED, antioxidant agents or topical alprostadil, and daily tadalafil with an on-demand short-acting PDE5I.

special_populations.population: Men with ED and suspected testosterone deficiency
special_populations.considerations: Symptoms suggesting hypogonadism should be assessed in men with ED. Studies cited by the guideline indicate that hypogonadal men who have not responded to PDE5Is may respond better after testosterone therapy.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: When diagnostic criteria suggest testosterone deficiency, testosterone therapy may be more appropriate. It can also be considered when clinically indicated for men with low or low-normal testosterone and associated sexual difficulties.

special_populations.population: Men with ED following radical prostatectomy or other prostate cancer treatment
special_populations.considerations: ED is frequent after RP and can also follow radiotherapy or brachytherapy. The guideline advises discussing other possible sexual changes with patients receiving active prostate cancer treatment. Evidence does not establish that penile rehabilitation after nerve-sparing RP increases spontaneous recovery of EF, and data do not support a particular rehabilitation regimen.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Begin pro-erectile treatment as early as possible after radical prostatectomy, pelvic surgery or other curative prostate cancer treatment. PDE5Is are considered first-line after nerve-sparing surgery. Early VED use and VED combined with PDE5Is should be considered as treatment alternatives; intracavernous injections and penile implants are described when oral PDE5Is are ineffective or unsuitable.

special_populations.population: Young men with ED after pelvic or perineal trauma
special_populations.considerations: These patients may be candidates for potentially curative revascularisation. Penile pharmaco-arteriography must confirm stenosis, and dynamic infusion cavernosometry or cavernosography must exclude corporeal veno-occlusive dysfunction, which contraindicates revascularisation.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Surgical penile revascularisation may be considered when the stated vascular criteria are met.

special_populations.population: Well-informed older men with ED, infrequent sexual intercourse and comorbidity
special_populations.considerations: For those seeking non-invasive treatment without medication, a vacuum erection device may be particularly suitable. These devices are contraindicated in patients with bleeding disorders or receiving anticoagulant therapy.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: A vacuum erection device may be the treatment of choice when non-invasive, drug-free management is preferred.

special_populations.population: Men with ED and diabetes mellitus undergoing penile prosthesis implantation
special_populations.considerations: Diabetes mellitus is a risk factor for prosthesis infection. The guideline reports no RCT-defined glycated haemoglobin threshold for proceeding with implantation.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Careful patient selection is needed. In a retrospective analysis of men with diabetes receiving a Coloplast Titan™ implant, vancomycin plus gentamicin was the most effective antibiotic combination for implant dipping against postoperative infection and subsequent explantation or revision.

special_populations.population: Men with spinal cord injury undergoing penile prosthesis implantation
special_populations.considerations: Published series report a greater complication risk, with prosthesis infection in up to 16% of cases.

special_populations.population: Men with ED and limited manual dexterity or high risk of complications from reservoir placement
special_populations.considerations: Limited manual dexterity can affect implant selection. Previous abdominal surgery is an example of a circumstance associated with concern about reservoir placement.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: A semi-rigid prosthesis may be an option for limited manual dexterity; a two-piece inflatable prosthesis may be an option when reservoir placement poses a high complication risk.

special_populations.population: Men who have sex with men presenting with ED
special_populations.considerations: The guideline notes psychological risks related to erectile capability during anal sex and calls for assessment tailored to sexual minorities.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with ED undergoing an individualised treatment assessment.
decision_rules: Discuss the patient's needs, expectations and preferences before selecting treatment; consider invasiveness, effectiveness, tolerability, safety and cost.
Identify and manage potentially reversible causes and ensure that associated endocrine, metabolic and cardiovascular conditions are adequately controlled.
Begin lifestyle changes and modification of risk factors before or alongside ED-specific treatment.
Offer PDE5Is as first-line pharmacological treatment; select an agent and dosing pattern in light of anticipated intercourse frequency and the patient's experience.

recommended_regimens.name: PDE5Is
recommended_regimens.summary: Use as first-line treatment for ED. Explain how the medicines work and how to take them, since incorrect use or insufficient instruction is a principal cause of apparent non-response.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The guideline reports a significant improvement in EF with a generally favourable safety profile and no demonstrated efficacy difference among the different PDE5Is.

recommended_regimens.name: Lifestyle changes and risk factor modification
recommended_regimens.summary: Introduce physical activity, weight management and management of modifiable risk factors before or concurrently with ED treatment.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Lifestyle changes can improve ED in specific populations.

alternative_regimens.name: Intracavernous injections
alternative_regimens.summary: May be offered as an alternative first-line treatment following adequate patient information.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: A well-informed patient chooses injections rather than oral first-line treatment.

alternative_regimens.name: Topical/intra-urethral alprostadil
alternative_regimens.summary: A less-invasive alternative first-line treatment; efficacy data remain limited.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The informed patient does not want, or is unsuitable for, oral vasoactive treatment; does not want intracavernous injections; or prefers a less-invasive option.

alternative_regimens.name: Vacuum erection devices
alternative_regimens.summary: A non-invasive, drug-free treatment option.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An informed patient requests management without medication or an invasive intervention.

response_assessment.method: Assess EF improvement, adverse effects, satisfaction and the patient's perception of treatment invasiveness.
response_assessment.interpretation: Treatment success includes patient satisfaction as well as efficacy and safety.

response_assessment.method: Check whether the chosen treatment was used correctly, give further instruction and counselling, and reassess satisfaction.
response_assessment.interpretation: Consider another attempt, an alternative treatment or combined therapies if the result remains inadequate.

supportive_care: Provide education and counselling to the patient and, when appropriate, the partner.
Use shared decision-making and consider combined psychosexual and medical or physical treatment.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline's algorithm is individualised rather than a mandatory sequence of three treatment tiers.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men choosing on-demand oral treatment for ED.
decision_rules: Adjust the starting dose according to clinical response and adverse effects.
Advise on dose, timing and the need for sexual stimulation; a high-fat meal can delay absorption of sildenafil, vardenafil and avanafil.
Two meta-analyses identified sildenafil 50 mg as the option for patients prioritising efficacy and tadalafil 10 mg as the initial option for those prioritising tolerability.

recommended_regimens.name: Sildenafil
recommended_regimens.summary: On-demand PDE5I; the recommended starting dose is 50 mg, adjusted for response and adverse effects. Available doses are 25, 50 and 100 mg. An orally disintegrating tablet is available in 25, 50, 75 and 100 mg, particularly for patients who have difficulty swallowing solid formulations; an oral suspension has also been developed.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a 24-week dose-response study, improved erections were reported by 56%, 77% and 84% of general ED patients taking 25, 50 and 100 mg sildenafil, respectively, versus 25% taking placebo.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: The effectiveness window begins 30-60 minutes after administration and extends up to 12 hours.

recommended_regimens.name: Tadalafil
recommended_regimens.summary: On-demand PDE5I given at 10 or 20 mg; begin with 10 mg and adapt to response and adverse effects.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a 12-week dose-response study, improved erections were reported by 67% and 81% of men taking 10 and 20 mg tadalafil, respectively, versus 35% taking placebo.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Effectiveness begins 30 minutes after administration, reaches peak efficacy after approximately 2 hours and lasts up to 36 hours.

recommended_regimens.name: Vardenafil
recommended_regimens.summary: On-demand PDE5I available at 5, 10 and 20 mg; the recommended starting dose is 10 mg, with subsequent adjustment for response and adverse effects. An orodispersable tablet is also available.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a 12-week dose-response study, improved erections were reported by 66%, 76% and 80% of men taking 5, 10 and 20 mg vardenafil, respectively, versus 30% taking placebo. One of three patients achieved satisfactory erections within 15 minutes of ingestion.

recommended_regimens.name: Avanafil
recommended_regimens.summary: On-demand PDE5I available at 50, 100 and 200 mg; start with 100 mg and adapt the dose according to efficacy and tolerability.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a general ED population, the mean percentages of successful sexual attempts resulting in intercourse were 47%, 58% and 59% with 50, 100 and 200 mg, respectively, versus 28% with placebo.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Take as needed 15-30 minutes before sexual activity.

not_recommended.name: PDE5Is with organic nitrates or NO donors
not_recommended.reason: Concomitant use is absolutely contraindicated because cGMP accumulation can cause unpredictable blood-pressure reductions and hypotensive symptoms; this includes recreational amyl nitrite or nitrate.

not_recommended.name: PDE5Is with nicorandil
not_recommended.reason: Concomitant use is contraindicated because the nitric oxide-donating action of nicorandil can raise cGMP levels.

response_assessment.method: Assess whether erection rigidity permits satisfactory intercourse, alongside tolerability and patient satisfaction.
response_assessment.interpretation: An apparently ineffective treatment warrants a review of correct prescribing and use before declaring non-response.

supportive_care: Explain correct dosing, timing and sexual stimulation.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Co-administration with antihypertensive agents can cause small, usually minor, additive reductions in blood pressure. The guideline reports no current restriction on simultaneous α-blockers and PDE5I use, while acknowledging potential haemodynamic changes.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men who prefer spontaneous rather than scheduled sexual activity, anticipate frequent sexual activity, or have concomitant LUTS/BPH.
decision_rules: Consider continuous tadalafil according to patient preference and physician judgement; reassess periodically whether daily dosing remains appropriate.
Consider tadalafil 5 mg in men with ED and mild to moderate LUTS, either alone or with α-blockers.
Daily treatment can also be considered when response to on-demand PDE5I treatment is partial.

recommended_regimens.name: Tadalafil
recommended_regimens.summary: For daily treatment, the EMA considers tadalafil 2.5 or 5 mg once daily suitable according to patient choice and clinical judgement; the recommended dose in these patients is 5 mg once daily at approximately the same time each day. It can provide a single treatment for ED with concomitant LUTS.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Among men aged > 45 years receiving tadalafil 5 mg once daily, 40% responded for both ED and LUTS/BPH, with symptom improvement after 12 weeks. The guideline reports no clinically significant difference between continuous once-daily and on-demand tadalafil treatment.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Once daily; periodically reassess continued use.

alternative_regimens.name: On-demand tadalafil
alternative_regimens.summary: An alternative to continuous tadalafil when dosing linked to anticipated sexual activity is acceptable.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The patient does not prefer or require continuous dosing.

response_assessment.method: Review EF, urinary symptoms when present, tolerability and the continuing suitability of daily administration.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline states that tadalafil 5 mg is licensed for both ED and LUTS. Combination with α-blockers calls for awareness of possible cumulative blood-pressure effects, although the cited meta-analysis did not find an increased rate of adverse events due to hypotension.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with ED and psychological, psychosexual or relationship factors for whom a psychosocial intervention is indicated.
decision_rules: Assess psychosexual history, life stressors, cultural context, relationship factors and thinking patterns concerning sexual performance.
When indicated, refer for Cognitive Behaviour Therapy, include the partner and combine the intervention with medical treatment to maximise outcomes.

recommended_regimens.name: Cognitive Behaviour Therapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Use as an indicated psychological treatment, with partner involvement and alongside medical ED treatment. Group, couple and online formats are described.

alternative_regimens.name: Psychosocial interventions
alternative_regimens.summary: Described approaches include sexual skills training, marital therapy and psychosexual education.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Tailor the approach to the patient's psychological, sexual and relationship needs.

response_assessment.method: Include relationship and intimacy, sexual satisfaction, well-being, and flexibility of thinking and expectations as psychosexual outcomes.

supportive_care: Educate the patient and partner about sexual response, ED, diagnostic findings and the reasons for selecting treatment.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Tailor psychosexual assessment to sexual minorities, including MSM, where relevant.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with low or low-normal testosterone levels and concomitant problems involving sexual desire, EF or satisfaction with intercourse or overall sex life.
decision_rules: Consider testosterone therapy when clinically indicated.

If diagnostic criteria suggest testosterone deficiency in a patient responding poorly to PDE5Is, testosterone therapy may be more appropriate; cited studies report that it may improve subsequent PDE5I response.

alternative_regimens.name: Testosterone therapy
alternative_regimens.summary: May be considered by intramuscular, transdermal or oral administration when the stated clinical indications are present, including in patients with a history of CVD.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Low or low-normal testosterone levels with the specified concomitant sexual symptoms, when treatment is clinically indicated.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with an apparently inadequate response to PDE5Is.
decision_rules: Identify why treatment appears ineffective: verify the prescription, licensed status of the product, correct administration, dose, timing and sexual stimulation.
Consider whether a high-fat meal has delayed absorption of sildenafil, vardenafil or avanafil, or whether intercourse was attempted too soon or too late.
After education, try the relevant PDE5I again before concluding that treatment has failed.
Consider testosterone therapy when diagnostic criteria suggest testosterone deficiency.
In refractory, complex or difficult-to-treat ED, consider combination treatment as an initial approach to that situation.

recommended_regimens.name: PDE5Is
recommended_regimens.summary: Correct prescribing and administration problems, counsel about dose, timing and stimulation, then repeat treatment with the relevant PDE5I.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Cited studies suggest that education and correct readministration can restore EF in some apparent non-responders.

alternative_regimens.name: PDE5Is with antioxidant agents
alternative_regimens.summary: One combination strategy considered for refractory, complex or difficult-to-treat ED; supporting combination data remain limited.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Persistent inadequate response after appropriate assessment and instruction.

alternative_regimens.name: PDE5Is with LI-SWT
alternative_regimens.summary: A possible combination strategy in difficult-to-treat ED.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: A refractory patient for whom LI-SWT is suitable.

alternative_regimens.name: PDE5Is with a vacuum erection device (VED)
alternative_regimens.summary: A possible combination strategy in refractory ED.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Persistent inadequate response when combined treatment is being considered.

alternative_regimens.name: Daily tadalafil with an on-demand short-acting PDE5I
alternative_regimens.summary: A combination strategy described for difficult-to-treat cases, using an on-demand agent such as sildenafil.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Persistent inadequate response in a refractory or complex case.

alternative_regimens.name: Li-SWT with VED
alternative_regimens.summary: A possible combined physical-treatment strategy.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: A refractory, complex or difficult-to-treat case.

alternative_regimens.name: PDE5Is with topical alprostadil
alternative_regimens.summary: A possible combined pharmacological strategy.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: A refractory, complex or difficult-to-treat case.

alternative_regimens.name: Intracavernous injections
alternative_regimens.summary: An established second-line option when oral treatment is insufficient.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Continued inadequate response to correctly used oral treatment.

response_assessment.method: Reassess EF, correct use, adverse effects and satisfaction.
response_assessment.interpretation: If the outcome remains inadequate, consider an alternative or combined therapy.

supportive_care: Provide renewed practical instructions and counselling.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Limited data suggest that an individual may respond differently to another PDE5I, but the guideline states that available RCTs have not reported evidence supporting a benefit from switching.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Well-informed men who do not want or are unsuitable for oral vasoactive treatment, do not want intracavernous injections, or prefer a less-invasive option.
decision_rules: Offer topical or intra-urethral alprostadil as an alternative first-line option under the stated preference or eligibility conditions.
For an intra-urethral pellet, begin at 500 μg; increase to 1000 μg if the clinical response is unsatisfactory.

alternative_regimens.name: Topical alprostadil
alternative_regimens.summary: A cream administered at the urethral meatus; formulations contain 200 and 300 μg. Topical alprostadil (VITAROSTM) at 300 μg is available in some European countries. Clinical efficacy data remain limited.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The patient meets the criteria for a less-invasive alternative to oral treatment or injections.

alternative_regimens.name: Intra-urethral alprostadil
alternative_regimens.summary: A medicated urethral pellet (MUSE™); the stated formulation range is 1251000 μg. Start at 500 μg and, if response is unsatisfactory, increase to 1000 μg.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The patient prefers an option less invasive than intracavernous injections while accepting lower efficacy.

response_assessment.method: Assess whether an erection sufficient for intercourse is achieved and review local adverse effects, dizziness and hypotension.
response_assessment.interpretation: For intra-urethral alprostadil, an unsatisfactory response to 500 μg permits escalation to 1000 μg.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The formal recommendation has strength Weak. With intra-urethral alprostadil, intercourse-sufficient erections occur in 30-65.9% of patients; efficacy is significantly lower than with intracavernous pharmacotherapy, and long-term adherence is 30%.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Well-informed men seeking non-invasive, drug-free treatment; the guideline also identifies older men with infrequent intercourse and comorbidity as potential candidates.
decision_rules: Use vacuum erection devices when an informed patient requests drug-free, non-invasive treatment.
Do not use vacuum erection devices in patients with bleeding disorders or receiving anticoagulant therapy.

alternative_regimens.name: Vacuum erection devices
alternative_regimens.summary: A drug-free treatment that may be particularly suitable for informed older patients with infrequent sexual intercourse and relevant comorbidity.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The patient requests non-invasive treatment and has neither a bleeding disorder nor anticoagulant therapy.

not_recommended.name: Vacuum erection devices in patients with bleeding disorders or on anticoagulant therapy
not_recommended.reason: The guideline identifies these circumstances as contraindications.

response_assessment.method: Assess erections adequate for intercourse, satisfaction, adverse effects and continued use.
response_assessment.interpretation: Published efficacy is as high as 90%; satisfaction ranges from 27% to 94%, and use falls to 50-64% after two years.

supportive_care: Instruct patients to remove the constriction ring within 30 minutes to avoid serious skin injury.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The formal recommendation has strength Weak.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men requiring injection treatment after inadequate response to another option, or well-informed men who choose injections as an alternative first-line treatment.
decision_rules: Offer intracavernous injections either as an alternative first-line treatment or as second-line treatment.
Provide supervised instruction in injection technique and close follow-up to address early discontinuation.
Avoid intracavernous alprostadil in men with hypersensitivity to alprostadil, risk of priapism or bleeding disorders.

recommended_regimens.name: Alprostadil
recommended_regimens.summary: Approved intracavernous monotherapy at 5-40 μg; 40 μg may be offered off label in some European countries. Teach the injection technique in an office-training programme.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Efficacy rates of > 70% are reported in general ED and in subgroups including men with diabetes or CVD. Reported satisfaction is 87-93.5% among patients and 86-90.3% among partners. Intracavernous pharmacotherapy has reported drop-out rates of 41-68%.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Erection begins after 5-15 minutes; duration depends on the injected dose and varies substantially between patients.

alternative_regimens.name: Bimix
alternative_regimens.summary: A combination of papaverine 7.5-45 mg and phentolamine 0.25-1.5 mg. It has been used for ED but has never been licensed for this indication.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider an intracavernous combination where available, with its unlicensed status made clear.

alternative_regimens.name: Trimix
alternative_regimens.summary: A combination of papaverine 8-16 mg, phentolamine 0.2-0.4 mg and alprostadil 10-20 μg. The guideline reports efficacy reaching 92% and less penile pain than alprostadil monotherapy, but it has never been licensed for ED.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider a combination injection where available, with its unlicensed status and fibrosis risk made clear.

alternative_regimens.name: InvicorpTM
alternative_regimens.summary: Combines vasoactive intestinal peptide (25 μg) with phentolamine mesylate (1-2 mg Invicorp). Clinical studies report effectiveness in > 80% of men with ED, including previous non-responders, with little penile pain and a virtually negligible risk of priapism.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider a combination injection where available, including after inadequate response to other therapies.

not_recommended.name: Papaverine monotherapy
not_recommended.reason: Its high incidence of adverse effects has led to its abandonment as monotherapy; papaverine is not licensed for ED.

not_recommended.name: Phentolamine monotherapy
not_recommended.reason: It produces a poor erectile response as monotherapy and is not licensed for ED.

response_assessment.timepoint: After initiation and during close follow-up
response_assessment.method: Assess erection quality, pain, prolonged erections, priapism, fibrosis, satisfaction and continued participation in the injection programme.
response_assessment.interpretation: Most reported discontinuations of intracavernous pharmacotherapy occur within the first two to three months.

supportive_care: Provide office-based injection training, careful counselling and close follow-up.
For alprostadil-related pain, the guideline describes sodium bicarbonate or local anaesthesia as possible measures.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline reports that 5-10% of patients do not respond even to combination intracavernous injections. Cavernosal fibrosis usually resolves after a temporary treatment interruption; tunical fibrosis may indicate early Peyronie’s disease and a need to stop injections indefinitely.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with mild vasculogenic ED, informed men who cannot or do not wish to use oral vasoactive therapy, or men with vasculogenic ED who respond poorly to PDE5Is.
decision_rules: Consider LI-SWT, with or without PDE5Is, for the populations specified in the weak formal recommendation.
Explain that improvement is generally modest and that treatment protocols and devices differ substantially.

alternative_regimens.name: LI-SWT
alternative_regimens.summary: May be used with or without PDE5Is in the specified vasculogenic ED populations. The formal recommendation has strength Weak.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Mild vasculogenic ED; an informed patient who does not wish to use or is unsuitable for oral vasoactive treatment; or vasculogenic ED with poor PDE5I response.

response_assessment.timepoint: One to three months after treatment completion and subsequently
response_assessment.method: Assess patient-reported EF, including IIEF and EHS where used, and whether improvement is satisfactory.
response_assessment.interpretation: Most studies suggest modest improvement, with satisfactory improvement reported by 40-80% of patients. Benefit tends to diminish over time, although effects have been detected up to five years after treatment.

supportive_care: Counsel about uncertainty arising from differing shockwave generators, wave types, settings and protocols.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: A cited RCT of radial wave therapy found no difference from placebo in IIEF-EF or EHS. The clinical meaning of reported improvements in penile haemodynamic measurements remains unclear.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with mild ED who decline pharmacological treatment after counselling.
decision_rules: Counsel that any EF improvement from the specified supplements may be mild before considering daily use.

alternative_regimens.name: L-arginine
alternative_regimens.summary: May be used daily under the conditions of the Weak formal recommendation. A cited meta-analysis reported a mean IIEF-EF increase of 2.74 (95%CI 1.67,3.81) compared with placebo, without a difference in sexual satisfaction score.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Mild ED with refusal of pharmacological treatment after counselling about a potentially mild benefit.

alternative_regimens.name: ginseng
alternative_regimens.summary: May be used daily under the conditions of the Weak formal recommendation. A cited Cochrane review found that effects on EF or intercourse satisfaction may be trivial compared with placebo.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Mild ED with refusal of pharmacological treatment after counselling about a potentially mild benefit.

response_assessment.method: Ask whether the patient perceives a meaningful improvement in EF and sexual satisfaction.
response_assessment.interpretation: The guideline cautions that a small measured improvement may not be meaningful to patients.

supportive_care: Explain the limited evidence on the efficacy, safety and clinical significance of herbal products and supplements.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with ED considering PRP, stem cells or BoNT-A, including patients unresponsive to established treatments where studied.
decision_rules: Restrict intracavernous PRP for ED to a clinical trial setting.
Do not present stem cells or BoNT-A as established clinical treatments: the guideline states that available evidence does not permit a clinical recommendation for either.

not_recommended.name: Intracavernous PRP in routine clinical practice
not_recommended.reason: Evidence remains insufficient for a clinical-practice recommendation despite some promising findings; studies vary in timing and dose, and larger trials are needed to establish efficacy and safety. The guideline states that use should be limited to clinical trials.

not_recommended.name: Stem cells as an established clinical treatment for ED
not_recommended.reason: Data are insufficient for a clinical recommendation; the placebo-controlled trials were small and yielded conflicting efficacy findings.

not_recommended.name: BoNT-A in routine clinical practice for ED
not_recommended.reason: Although results in treatment non-responders are promising, larger trials are needed to establish efficacy and safety before a clinical-practice recommendation can be given.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: A cited meta-analysis of PRP RCTs reported a mean IIEF-EF improvement versus placebo of 3.21 [95%CI: 1.82; 4.60] 6 months after treatment; this does not change the guideline's clinical-trial-only restriction.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men following radical prostatectomy/pelvic surgery or other curative treatment for prostate cancer, particularly after nerve-sparing surgery.
decision_rules: Discuss sexual effects of active prostate cancer treatment beyond ED, including changes in desire, orgasm, ejaculation, penile shape and penile size.
Start pro-erectile treatment at the earliest opportunity after radical prostatectomy/pelvic surgery or another curative prostate cancer treatment.
Consider PDE5Is first-line after nerve-sparing surgery, irrespective of surgical technique.
Do not promise that a particular penile rehabilitation regimen will restore spontaneous, unassisted EF.

recommended_regimens.name: PDE5Is
recommended_regimens.summary: First-line ED treatment after nerve-sparing surgery; early initiation of pro-erectile treatment after surgery or another curative prostate cancer treatment carries a separate Weak recommendation.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The guideline's evidence summary states that penile rehabilitation with PDE5Is after RP does not increase the chance of spontaneous EF recovery. A cited Cochrane review found little or no short-term self-reported potency benefit from scheduled PDE5Is versus placebo or no treatment and no increase in self-reported EF versus on-demand use; a different, updated meta-analysis identified daily sildenafil 100 mg as the most effective of its compared strategies for EF recovery after RP.

alternative_regimens.name: Vacuum erection devices
alternative_regimens.summary: Early VED use is described by a cited meta-analysis as a therapeutic alternative after RP.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider when a non-drug or additional treatment is appropriate after RP.

alternative_regimens.name: VED and PDE5is
alternative_regimens.summary: A cited analysis found advantages for combined treatment over monotherapy after RP and the guideline says this combination should be considered.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: ED after RP when combined treatment is appropriate.

alternative_regimens.name: Intracavernous injections
alternative_regimens.summary: Described as second-line treatment after RP.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Oral PDE5Is are insufficiently effective or unsuitable.

alternative_regimens.name: Penile implants
alternative_regimens.summary: Described as third-line treatment after RP.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Oral treatment is unsuitable or inadequate and the patient progresses to an implant-based option.

alternative_regimens.name: PFMT combined with bio-feedback
alternative_regimens.summary: A cited systematic review described this as a promising non-pharmacological alternative but called for better-powered, rigorous RCTs.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider in the context of the limited evidence identified by the review.

response_assessment.method: Assess EF, ability to resume sexual activity, treatment satisfaction and whether erections occur without pharmacological assistance.
response_assessment.interpretation: The evidence does not establish that penile rehabilitation itself raises the likelihood of spontaneous EF recovery after nerve-sparing RP.

supportive_care: Proactively discuss ED and other sexual dysfunction after RP and offer treatment options.
Explain that evidence is inadequate to support a particular penile rehabilitation regimen; this information carries a Weak formal recommendation.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Age, baseline EF and the quality of nerve preservation are identified as important influences on post-RP EF and PDE5I outcomes. The guideline also gives a Strong recommendation to discuss sexual changes other than ED with patients receiving active prostate cancer treatment.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Young men with post-traumatic arteriogenic ED following pelvic or perineal trauma.
decision_rules: Consider surgical penile revascularisation only after confirming stenosis by penile pharmaco-arteriography.
Exclude corporeal veno-occlusive dysfunction with dynamic infusion cavernosometry or cavernosography before revascularisation.

alternative_regimens.name: Surgical penile revascularisation
alternative_regimens.summary: A potentially curative surgical option for appropriately selected young patients with pelvic or perineal trauma.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Confirmed arterial stenosis without corporeal veno-occlusive dysfunction.

not_recommended.name: Surgical penile revascularisation with corporeal veno-occlusive dysfunction
not_recommended.reason: The guideline identifies corporeal veno-occlusive dysfunction as a contraindication.

response_assessment.method: Assess sustained restoration of erectile function.
response_assessment.interpretation: The guideline reports a 60-70% long-term success rate for surgical penile revascularisation in young patients with pelvic or perineal trauma.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men who do not respond to other treatments, are unsuitable for pharmacotherapies, or prefer a definitive intervention.
decision_rules: Consider a penile prosthesis after failure of other treatments or in accordance with patient preference, following full discussion of benefits and harms.

Individualise the implant type and operative approach. A two-piece inflatable prosthesis may suit a patient at high risk from reservoir placement, while a semi-rigid device may suit a man with limited manual dexterity.
Discuss infection, mechanical failure and other operative complications before implantation.

recommended_regimens.name: Penile prosthesis
recommended_regimens.summary: Implant when other treatments have failed or according to patient preference, with comprehensive counselling. Options described include inflatable two- and three-piece devices and semi-rigid devices; the guideline does not establish superior efficacy or safety for a particular implant or surgical approach.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: With appropriate counselling, reported satisfaction is 92-100% among patients and 91-95% among partners. A cited meta-analysis reported implant durability or survival of 93.3% at 1 year, 91.0% at 3 years, 87.2% at 5 years, 76.8% at 10 years, 63.7% at 15 years and 52.9% at 20 years.

not_recommended.name: Venous ligation surgery
not_recommended.reason: The guideline no longer recommends it for veno-occlusive dysfunction because long-term results are poor.

response_assessment.method: Assess device function, patient and partner satisfaction, infection, erosion and other complications.
response_assessment.interpretation: Mechanical failure rates of < 5% after 5 years of follow-up are reported for modified commonly used three-piece prostheses.

supportive_care: Provide appropriate antibiotic prophylaxis against Gram-positive and negative bacteria and use careful surgical technique.
The guideline describes coated prostheses and techniques limiting wound exposure and skin contact as measures that appear to reduce infection rates.
Consider focused psychosexual counselling for the patient and partner after implantation.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Diabetes mellitus, hypogonadism and spinal cord injury are discussed as infection or complication risk factors. The guideline states that no RCT has established an acceptable preoperative glycated-haemoglobin threshold for patients with diabetes.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with an infected penile prosthesis.
decision_rules: Remove the infected prosthesis and administer antibiotics.
As an alternative, consider immediate salvage with wash-out and insertion of a new prosthesis after discussing the advantages and disadvantages with the patient.
Do not apply a universal rule for management after explantation; individualise the decision through full consultation.

recommended_regimens.name: Prosthesis removal and antibiotic administration
recommended_regimens.summary: Manage prosthetic infection by explanting the infected device and giving antibiotics.

alternative_regimens.name: Immediate salvage and replacement with a new prosthesis
alternative_regimens.summary: Remove the infected device, apply a wash-out protocol and implant a replacement immediately; reported successful salvage exceeds > 80% of cases.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Individualised selection after full discussion of the benefits and disadvantages of salvage.

response_assessment.method: Assess resolution of infection and, where salvage is attempted, whether the replacement prosthesis is retained successfully.

supportive_care: Administer antibiotics for prosthetic infection.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline does not give an absolute recommendation choosing between delayed management after removal and immediate salvage.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with ED without overt cardiovascular disease or cardiac symptoms, particularly when a vasculogenic cause is suspected.
decision_rules: Assess standard cardiovascular risk and, for predominantly vasculogenic ED, calculate 10-year ASCVD risk.

For borderline to intermediate ASCVD risk, consider CAC assessment as proposed by the Princeton Consensus Conference IV; account for local expertise, test availability, cost-effectiveness and the patient's clinical profile.
Address cardiovascular risk factors and cardiovascular prevention alongside standard ED treatment.

recommended_regimens.name: Lifestyle changes and risk factor modification
recommended_regimens.summary: Emphasise lifestyle measures while evaluating and managing cardiovascular risk and ED.

response_assessment.timepoint: At initial cardiovascular assessment and subsequent reassessment
response_assessment.method: Calculate ASCVD risk and, where indicated, use CAC findings to inform cardiovascular prevention.
response_assessment.interpretation: The prose defines 10-year ASCVD categories as low risk < 5%, borderline risk 5% to < 7.5%, intermediate risk ≥ 7.5% to < 20%, and high risk ≥ 20%.

supportive_care: Educate and counsel the patient and, where appropriate, the partner.
Use shared decision-making and address lifestyle and cardiovascular risk factors.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The cardiovascular diagram presents simplified risk ranges that do not match every boundary in the prose: low risk (<5%), borderline to intermediate risk (5-20%) and high risk (>20%). It displays CAC = O, CAC 1 to 100 and CAC > 100, as well as prevention measures that include lifestyle emphasis; lifestyle modification, a moderate- to high-intensity statin aimed at LDL < 70 mg/dL and consideration of preventive cardiology; and a high-intensity statin aimed at LDL < 70 mg/dL, consideration of aspirin and preventive-cardiology referral. The diagram does not clearly connect each measure to an individual CAC category.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with overt cardiovascular symptoms and/or CVD whose risk associated with sexual activity requires assessment.
decision_rules: Classify the cardiovascular risk of sexual activity before advising on ED treatment.

For intermediate or indeterminable risk, perform exercise stress testing before resumption of sexual activity; a chemical stress test with echocardiography or nuclear imaging may be used when a standard exercise test cannot be completed.
Refer high-risk patients, or those whose stress test indicates high risk, for cardiological assessment; a low-risk result permits advice and ED treatment.
Assess the necessity of nitrates before considering PDE5Is. If nitrates remain necessary, use a non-PDE5Is ED treatment; the diagram considers PDE5Is when the patient is off nitrates.

alternative_regimens.name: PDE5Is
alternative_regimens.summary: An oral ED treatment option after cardiovascular risk assessment when contraindicating concomitant treatment is absent.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The patient is suitable for ED treatment and is not taking necessary nitrates or another contraindicated concomitant medicine.

alternative_regimens.name: Non-PDE5Is RX for ED
alternative_regimens.summary: The cardiovascular management diagram directs patients requiring nitrates toward non-PDE5Is ED treatment.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Nitrates are necessary and therefore cannot be stopped.

not_recommended.name: PDE5Is with organic nitrates
not_recommended.reason: The guideline identifies concomitant nitrate use as an absolute contraindication because of potentially unpredictable hypotension.

not_recommended.name: PDE5Is with nicorandil
not_recommended.reason: Concomitant use is contraindicated because of the potential increase in cGMP levels.

response_assessment.timepoint: Before resuming sexual activity when risk is indeterminable
response_assessment.method: Use exercise stress testing, or the described alternative stress testing when exercise testing is not possible.
response_assessment.interpretation: The management diagram routes a failed test to high-risk management and cardiologist referral, and a passed test to low-risk advice and ED treatment.

response_assessment.method: Assess EF improvement, adverse effects, patient satisfaction and adequacy of treatment use.
response_assessment.interpretation: If the outcome is inadequate, give further instruction and consider an alternative or combined treatment.

supportive_care: Provide education and counselling to the patient and, where appropriate, the partner.
Address lifestyle and cardiovascular risk factors and use shared decision-making.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline defines low-risk profiles as including successfully revascularized individuals, controlled asymptomatic hypertension, mild valvular disease and specified NYHA classes I and II patients achieving 5 METS without ischaemia. document_sections.heading: 4. EPIDEMIOLOGY AND PREVALENCE OF SEXUAL DYSFUNCTION AND DISORDERS OF MALE REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH
document_sections.content: This chapter describes the frequency of erectile, ejaculatory and sexual-desire problems in men. Estimates vary across populations, definitions and study methods.

document_sections.heading: 4.1 Erectile dysfunction
document_sections.content: ED is prevalent worldwide. The Massachusetts Male Aging Study (MMAS) found ED in 52% of noninstitutionalised Boston-area men aged 40-70 years: minimal ED in 17.2%, moderate ED in 25.2% and complete ED in 9.6%. The Cologne study found ED in 19.2% of men aged 30-80 years, with age-related prevalence rising from 2.3% to 53.4%. Annual incidence per 1,000 men was 26 in long-term MMAS data and 19.2 in a Dutch study with a mean follow-up of 4.2 years. Among men first seeking care for newly developed ED, one in four was younger than 40 years; almost 50% of these younger men described severe ED. Differences between estimates may reflect methodology, age and the socio-economic and cultural characteristics of study populations. Additional prevalence estimates appear in Appendix 2 Table S4.1.

document_sections.heading: 4.2 Premature ejaculation
document_sections.content: The National Health and Social Life Survey (NHSLS) reported PE in 31% of men aged 18-59 years in the USA. Its age-specific estimates were 30% at 18-29 years, 32% at 30-39 years, 28% at 40-49 years and 55% at 50-59 years. The document questions whether actual PE prevalence reaches 20-30%, given how few affected men seek care. A single yes/no question about ejaculating too early may explain the high survey estimates; European studies reported significantly lower prevalence. Two observational cross-sectional surveys on different continents found overall rates of 19.8 and 25.8%, respectively. Applying the classifications of Waldinger et al., their respective rates were 2.3 and 3.18% for lifelong PE, 3.9 and 4.48% for acquired PE, 8.5 and 11.38% for variable PE, and 5.1 and 6.4% for subjective PE. In both surveys, men with acquired PE sought treatment more often than men with lifelong PE. Appendix 2 Table S4.2 presents the markedly differing prevalence estimates.

document_sections.heading: 4.3 Other ejaculatory disorders
document_sections.content: The following sections address delayed ejaculation, anejaculation, anorgasmia, retrograde ejaculation, painful ejaculation and haemospermia.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.1 Delayed ejaculation
document_sections.content: Uncertain definitions make the epidemiology of delayed ejaculation (DE) unclear, although several well-designed studies estimate prevalence at around 3% among sexually active men. In the NHSLS national probability sample, 7.78% of 1,246 men aged 18-59 years said they could not achieve climax or ejaculation. In a British stratified national probability survey conducted over six months among 11,161 men and women aged 16-44 years, 0.7% of men reported inability to reach orgasm. An international survey of 13,618 men aged 40–80 years in 29 countries found that 1.1-2.8% frequently could not reach orgasm. In a USA national probability sample of 1,455 men aged 57-85 years, 20% reported inability to climax; 73% reported being troubled by it. DE may be lifelong, acquired or situational. On limited evidence, estimated prevalence is 1% for lifelong DE and 4% for acquired DE.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.2 Anejaculation and Anorgasmia
document_sections.content: Precise prevalence estimates are difficult because many men do not distinguish ejaculation from orgasm and both conditions are rare. In a USA report, 8% of men said they had been unable to achieve orgasm during the preceding year. Kinsey et al. estimated anejaculation in 0.14% of the general population. The most frequent causes reported were spinal cord injury, diabetes mellitus and multiple sclerosis. Medical assistance is the only means of ejaculation in most cases involving spinal cord injury. In patients with spinal cord injury, masturbation produces the lowest ejaculation rates; penile vibratory stimulation or acetylcholine esterase inhibitors followed by masturbation produce higher response rates.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.3 Retrograde ejaculation
document_sections.content: The true incidence of retrograde ejaculation (RE) is difficult to establish. RE is reported in 0.3-2% of fertility-clinic attendees. Diabetes may increase its occurrence through autonomic neuropathy, which can produce ED and ejaculatory problems spanning DE, RE and anejaculation according to the degree of sympathetic involvement. RE occurred at an incidence of 6% among 54 diabetic patients with sexual dysfunction, in 34.6% of diabetic men in a controlled trial, and in at least 8.8% of 57 patients with type-1-diabetes mellitus aged 18-50 years in another trial. RE has also been reported after transurethral resection of prostate (TURP) or open prostatectomy when bladder-neck integrity is disrupted. In a study assessing quality of life after TURP in 5,276 men, 68% reported postoperative RE. Its incidence after surgery for LUTS decreases with less invasive techniques.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.4 Painful ejaculation
document_sections.content: Painful ejaculation is a common, poorly understood phenomenon associated with sexual dysfunction. Studies report prevalence of 1-10% in the general population and potentially 30-75% among men with chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome (CP/CPPS). Most studies had scientifically weak designs. The condition was probably under-reported because an evidence-based definition and clear prognostic criteria were lacking.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.5 Haemospermia
document_sections.content: Its concealed presentation, usual spontaneous resolution and patient embarrassment complicate estimation of haemospermia incidence and prevalence. It accounts for 1-1.5% of urological referrals, occurs across age groups and has a mean presentation age of 37 years. At enrolment in a PCa screening study of 26,126 men aged > 50 years or older than 40 with a PCa history or black ethnicity, 0.5% had haemospermia.

document_sections.heading: 4.4 Low sexual desire
document_sections.content: Reported worldwide prevalence of low sexual desire in men is 3-28%. Low solitary desire was reported in 68% of men and low dyadic desire in 14%. Among gay men, reported prevalence is 19-57%. Although associated with age, low desire also occurs among men aged 18-29 years, with reported prevalence of 6-19%.

document_sections.heading: 5. MANAGEMENT OF ERECTILE DYSFUNCTION
document_sections.content: This chapter addresses the definition, causes, diagnostic evaluation, treatment and follow-up of ED.

document_sections.heading: 5.1 Definition and classification
document_sections.content: ED means a persistent inability to obtain and sustain an erection adequate for satisfying sexual activity. It can harm psychosocial health and substantially affect patients’ and partners’ quality of life. The customary aetiological categories are organic, psychogenic and mixed, but that division needs caution because most cases involve both types of factors. The terms “primary organic” and “primary psychogenic” have consequently been proposed.

document_sections.heading: 5.2 Risk factors
document_sections.content: Vascular, hormonal, neurological and psychological disturbances can contribute to ED, which is also associated with chronic illness. Reported risk factors include age, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia, hypertension, CVD, obesity, MetS, hyperhomocysteinemia, inactivity, smoking and drug use. Some CVD medicines adversely affect erectile function (EF), while newer agents may have neutral or beneficial effects. Other reported associations include atrial fibrillation, hyperthyroidism, vitamin D or folic acid deficiency, hyperuricemia, depression, anxiety disorders, chronic kidney or rheumatic disease, COPD, migraine, inflammatory bowel disease, osteoporosis and sleep disorders. Growing evidence links newly arising ED with prior COVID-19. ED also commonly accompanies LUTS/BPH and its surgical treatment, chronic pelvic pain syndrome (CPPS), chronic prostatitis, bladder pain syndrome/interstitial cystitis, premature ejaculation and urethroplasty for posterior urethral strictures.

document_sections.heading: 5.3 Pathophysiology
document_sections.content: ED may involve vasculogenic, neurogenic, anatomical, hormonal, drug-induced or psychogenic mechanisms. Several mechanisms often coexist and can each impair EF. Table 5.1 organises the reported mechanisms and associated conditions, behaviours, procedures and medicines, including mixed and trauma-related pathways. A short-term symmetry analysis found that cardiovascular medicines did not strongly affect subsequent prescribing of anti-erectogenic medication; it assessed only short-term risk.

document_sections.heading: 5.3.1 Pelvic surgery and prostate cancer treatment
document_sections.content: Pelvic operations, especially radical prostatectomy (RP), radical cystectomy and colorectal cancer surgery, may impair EF and broader sexual health through injury to the neurovascular bundles, despite adoption of nerve-sparing techniques. Among these procedures, only PCa surgery currently has sufficient scientific evidence for a potential pathophysiological link with ED. PCa radiotherapy and brachytherapy can also be associated with ED. In the ProtecT trial, 1,643 patients with localised PCa were randomised to RP, RT or active monitoring; sexual function was assessed with EPIC-26. At baseline, 67% reported erections firm enough for intercourse. At six-year follow-up, this was 30% with active monitoring, 27%% with RT and 17% with RP. An RCT in low- to intermediate-risk PCa without ADT found significantly higher EPIC-26 sexual-function scores at two years after RT than after surgery. RP is widely used for clinically localised intermediate- or high-risk PCa. Studies report ED after RP in 25-75% of men, while unassisted postoperative EF recovery is 20 and 25% in most studies; these rates have changed little over the past two decades. Age, baseline EF, surgical volume, ability to spare neurovascular bundles and surgeon experience influence postoperative EF. Evidence comparing operative approaches conflicts: one systematic review favoured RARP over open retropubic RP for twelve-month potency, whereas two RCTs found only a small EF improvement with RARP or no difference. After EBRT, brachytherapy or both, a systematic review and meta-analysis found ED prevalence of 34% at one year and 57% at 5.5 years; its treatment groups comprised 65%, 31% and 4%, respectively. At five years after stereotactic radiotherapy, 26-55% of previously sexually functioning patients reported ED. Studies of HIFU, prostate cryotherapy, focal padeliporfin-based vascular-targeted photodynamic therapy and focal RT using brachytherapy or CyberKnife® report less adverse impact on EF, with many reporting complete recovery at one-year follow-up.

document_sections.heading: 5.3.2 Summary of evidence on the epidemiology/aetiology/pathophysiology of ED
document_sections.content: The evidence summary grades worldwide frequency of ED, shared cardiovascular risk factors, ED after RP, ED after external radiotherapy or brachytherapy, and lower ED frequency after cryotherapy or high-intensity focused US as LE 2b. Improvement in EF with regular exercise and lower BMI is LE 1b. The distinction that ED is a symptom rather than a disease, and that an underlying cause may go unevaluated or untreated, is LE 4.

document_sections.heading: 5.4 Diagnostic evaluation (basic work-up)
document_sections.content: The basic evaluation considers medical and sexual history, examination, laboratory assessment and, when appropriate, cardiovascular risk.

document_sections.heading: 5.4.1 Medical and sexual history
document_sections.content: Evaluation begins with a detailed medical and sexual history from the patient and, when available, the partner. Clinicians should characterise the firmness and duration of stimulated and morning erections and ask about desire, arousal, ejaculation and orgasm. Validated instruments such as IIEF and SHIM assess sexual-function domains and treatment effects; structured interviews help identify and quantify contributors to impaired EF. The Erectile Hardness Score (EHS) is supported for measuring penile rigidity in clinical care and research. Every patient should be screened for possible hypogonadal symptoms, including reduced libido, low energy and fatigue.

document_sections.heading: 5.4.2 Physical examination
document_sections.content: Every patient requires an examination focused on genitourinary, endocrine, vascular and neurological findings. This can uncover Peyronie’s disease, premalignant or malignant genital lesions, prostatic enlargement or irregularity, and indications of hypogonadism. Measure blood pressure and heart rate if not checked within the previous three to six months. Calculate BMI or measure waist circumference to evaluate associated conditions such as MetS.

document_sections.heading: 5.4.3 Laboratory testing
document_sections.content: If not assessed within the previous twelve months, obtain fasting blood glucose or haemoglobin A1c and a lipid profile. Hormonal assessment includes fasting early-morning total testosterone; bio-available or calculated-free testosterone may sometimes corroborate the total value. In selected patients, signs and symptoms may justify further tests, such as total PSA, PRL or LH. Examination and laboratory testing may not establish an exact diagnosis, but can reveal comorbidities.

document_sections.content: The diagram outlines history, validated sexual-function assessment, identification of causes and reversible risk factors, psychosocial assessment, focused examination and metabolic and hormonal testing. It includes assessment for other sexual problems, cardiovascular and neurological findings, hypogonadism, penile deformity and prostatic disease. Glucose and lipid testing is indicated if not performed in the last 12 months.

document_sections.heading: 5.4.4 Cardiovascular system and sexual activity: the patient at risk
document_sections.content: CVD is frequent among people seeking care for sexual dysfunction. ED significantly raises the risks of CVD, coronary heart disease, stroke, atrial fibrillation, cardiovascular death and death from any cause. In an observational population study of 965 men initially without CVD, transient or persistent ED in younger men, particularly those < 50 years, accompanied greater Framingham CVD risk. ED should therefore be regarded as a possible precursor to CVD; greater severity and duration indicate greater risk. It may improve detection of asymptomatic CVD with or without diabetes. The EAU approach adapts the 2024 Princeton Consensus Conference IV recommendations. That conference recommended the 2019 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association ASCVD risk score for all men assessed for predominantly vasculogenic ED. Its Pooled Cohort Equations (PCE) use age, sex, ethnicity, total cholesterol, HDL-cholesterol, systolic blood pressure, hypertension treatment, diabetes and smoking to estimate major cardiovascular events over the next 10 years. Categories are low risk < 5%, borderline risk 5% to < 7.5%, intermediate risk ≥ 7.5% to < 20% and high risk ≥ 20%. Because this tool alone can substantially underestimate risk in men aged 40 to 60 years, the Princeton expert panel recommended non-contrast cardiac computed tomography for coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring in men with borderline to intermediate ASCVD risk. The panel considered CAC its strongest single predictor of CVD risk for guiding clinical advice. Proposed pathways also evaluate sexual-activity risk in men with overt cardiovascular symptoms or established CVD, including ischaemic, rhythm and cardiac-output disorders, and address PDE5Is in low-risk men who use or can readily access nitrates. Apply these pathways according to local expertise, test availability, cost-effectiveness, European practice and individual clinical circumstances.

document_sections.heading: Figure 5.2: Cardiovascular risk assessment of ED patient with no overt disease or cardiac symptoms (based on IV Princeton Consensus) [334]
document_sections.content: The pathway begins with ED enquiry, cardiovascular assessment and consideration of a vasculogenic mechanism. For suspected vasculogenic ED it calculates 10-year ASCVD risk and considers risk-enhancing factors and shared decisions. Its displayed bands are low (<5%), borderline to intermediate (5-20%) and high (>20%). Borderline-to-intermediate assessment incorporates CAC testing; the diagram distinguishes CAC = O, CAC 1 to 100 and CAC > 100 and presents escalating lifestyle, lipid-lowering and preventive-cardiology responses, including LDL < 70 mg/dL targets in its higher CAC branches. ED management also considers counselling, PDE5Is, topical or intra-urethral alprostadil, LI-SWT and, after inadequate treatment outcomes, penile prosthesis implantation. Patient needs, partner involvement, side effects, satisfaction and adequacy of treatment use inform decisions.

document_sections.heading: Figure 5.3. Management of ED in men with overt CV symptoms and/or CVD (based on IV Princeton Consensus) [334]
document_sections.content: The pathway confirms ED, evaluates suspected vasculogenic disease and exercise ability, and separates low, intermediate or indeterminable, and high cardiovascular risk before treatment decisions. Intermediate or uncertain risk leads to stress testing; a failed test indicates high risk and cardiology referral, whereas a passed test indicates low risk. It also distinguishes whether nitrates or riociguat are being taken and whether nitrates remain necessary when considering PDE5Is or non-PDE5Is treatment. Low-risk patients can generally perform modest exercise without symptoms; examples include successful revascularisation, controlled asymptomatic hypertension, mild valve disease and NYHA classes I and II heart failure with 5 METS without ischaemia on recent testing. Intermediate or indeterminable profiles include mild or moderate stable angina, MI 2-8 weeks earlier without intervention while awaiting exercise electrocardiography, NYHA class III heart failure, peripheral arterial disease, and prior stroke or transient ischaemic attack. They require exercise stress testing before resuming sexual activity; inability to exercise may warrant chemical stress testing with echocardiography or nuclear imaging. Suspected atherosclerosis may warrant CAC, carotid intima-media thickness or ankle-brachial index to help reclassify risk. High-risk profiles include unstable or refractory angina, uncontrolled hypertension, NYHA class IV heart failure, MI without intervention < 2 weeks earlier, and high-risk arrhythmias. The pathway incorporates education, lifestyle measures, shared decisions, reassessment of inadequate treatment and possible penile prosthesis implantation.

document_sections.heading: 5.5 Diagnostic Evaluation (advanced work-up)
document_sections.content: History is sufficient to guide management for most patients with ED. Specific diagnostic investigations are appropriate for some patients, as outlined in Table 5.2.

document_sections.heading: 5.5.1 Nocturnal penile tumescence and rigidity test
document_sections.content: NPTR devices record nocturnal erection episodes, changes in circumference, peak penile rigidity and erection duration. Testing should cover at least two separate nights. An erection with tip rigidity of at least 60% lasting ≥ 10 minutes indicates a functional erectile mechanism. Normal NPTR findings are usual in psychogenic ED, so the test can help distinguish psychogenic from organic causes. Its routine diagnostic usefulness is limited by uncertainty about correspondence with sex-related erections, definitions of ED and potential confounding by situation, age, depression and sleep-related factors.

document_sections.heading: 5.5.2 Intracavernous injection test
document_sections.content: This test offers limited vascular information. A positive response is an unbendable erection beginning within 10 minutes after injection and lasting 30 minutes. By itself it does not establish a diagnosis; request penile duplex Doppler assessment when clinically warranted.

document_sections.heading: 5.5.3 Dynamic duplex ultrasound of the penis
document_sections.content: Dynamic penile duplex US is a second-level assessment of erectile haemodynamics, usually used when vasculogenic ED is suspected, such as with diabetes mellitus, multiple cardiovascular risks, evident peripheral vascular disease, renal transplantation or poor response to oral treatment. Normal values are peak systolic blood flow > 30 cm/s, end-diastolic velocity < 3 cm/s and resistance index > 0.8. Recent data suggest haemodynamic imaging might help tailor LI-SWT for vasculogenic ED. Normal findings make further vascular investigation unnecessary. Limitations include nonstandardised haemodynamic measures, false-positive diagnoses associated with anxiety or insufficient vasoactive dosing, and uncertain additional value beyond injection testing. Audiovisual sexual stimulation, higher-dose alprostadil or combinations of vasoactive and/or oral agents may improve accuracy.

document_sections.heading: 5.5.4 Arteriography and dynamic infusion cavernosometry or cavernosography
document_sections.content: Reserve pudendal arteriography for patients being considered for penile revascularisation. Dynamic infusion cavernosometry and cavernosography are now seldom used to investigate suspected venogenic ED, whose conceptual basis has been questioned. Computed tomography cavernosography is an emerging method that may supply anatomical detail for diagnosis and treatment planning.

document_sections.heading: 5.5.5 Psychopathological and psychosocial assessment
document_sections.content: Depression, anxiety and other psychological distress often coexist with ED; relevant problems may also be temporary mood changes associated with a particular crisis or stressor. Dissatisfaction with a partner, poor sexual relationships, relationship duration and emotional disconnection during sex have been linked to erectile difficulties, whereas intimacy has been identified as protective. Assessment must also address dysfunctional beliefs and expectations about sex, low self-esteem and distraction from erotic cues in organic and non-organic ED. Psychosexual evaluation includes an interview covering these issues; self-report measures are frequently used. Emerging data suggest that men who have sex with men (MSM) may have particular psychological risks concerning erections during anal sex, so evaluation must be tailored to sexual minorities.

document_sections.content: The diagram addresses life stressors, sexual and relationship history, cultural background, partner involvement, and beliefs about sexuality and EF. It includes deciding whether sexual psychotherapy is appropriate and evaluating relationship or intimacy, sexual satisfaction, well-being and flexibility of expectations as treatment outcomes.
