document_sections.content: The table identifies situations that may warrant specialised ED testing, including primary ED, selected younger patients after pelvic or perineal trauma, penile deformity, complex psychiatric, psychosexual or endocrine problems, patient or partner requests, and medico-legal circumstances. It lists nocturnal rigidity assessment, vascular investigations and specialised endocrine or psychodiagnostic evaluation.

document_sections.heading: 5.5.6 Summary of evidence and recommendations for diagnostic evaluation of ED
document_sections.content: History, examination and metabolic and hormonal laboratory assessment may identify ED risks and help clarify its cause (LE 3). Validated questionnaires such as IIEF and EHS reliably assess severity (LE 3); specialised tests may help distinguish vascular, hormonal and psychogenic causes (LE 3). Strong: obtain comprehensive medical and sexual histories for every patient, including focused enquiry about stressors, culture and sexual-performance cognitions. Strong: use a validated ED questionnaire to assess sexual-function domains and treatment effects. Strong: include focused examination at initial assessment to identify underlying illness and associated genital disorders. Strong: assess glucose, lipids and total testosterone to find treatable risks and modifiable lifestyle factors. Strong: include specific diagnostic tests during initial assessment when the indications in Table 5.2 apply.

document_sections.heading: 5.6 Treatment of erectile dysfunction
document_sections.content: The panel offers a personalised decision algorithm instead of the traditional three-tier model. Selection accounts for invasiveness, tolerability, effectiveness and patient expectations, and patients should receive counselling on every available modality. Most men do not receive cause-specific therapy; management therefore depends on invasiveness, efficacy, safety, cost and patient preference, with continuing clinician–patient dialogue. A systematic review found persistent discontinuation across ED treatments. Patient beliefs, perceived ineffectiveness, adverse effects, intimate-relationship quality and cost were prominent barriers to continuing treatment.

document_sections.heading: Figure 5.5: Management algorithm for erectile dysfunction
document_sections.content: The algorithm begins with comprehensive history, identification and treatment of potentially curable causes, lifestyle and risk-factor changes, education, partner involvement and shared decision-making. Options include PDE5Is, vacuum devices, topical or intra-urethral alprostadil and intracavernous injections; LI-SWT is restricted to vasculogenic ED. It accounts for definitive severe ED associated with major non-nerve-sparing pelvic surgery, neurological causes or trauma. Treatment review considers perceived invasiveness, EF improvement, adverse effects and satisfaction. If outcomes are inadequate, assess correct use, provide further instruction, retry or combine or change approaches, and consider a penile prosthesis when appropriate.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.1 Patient education
document_sections.content: Education is often the initial response to sexual concerns. Explaining the psychological and physiological aspects of sexual response in accessible terms has been shown to improve sexual satisfaction in men with ED. Consultation should address patient and partner needs and expectations, their understanding of ED and diagnostic findings, and the reasoning behind treatment selection.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.2 Modifiable risk factors
document_sections.content: Lifestyle and medication-related ED risk factors may be reversible or modifiable; address them before or alongside ED-specific therapy. Associated endocrine, metabolic and cardiovascular conditions, including diabetes and hypertension, should be well controlled as an initial treatment step. Studies suggest physical activity, particularly aerobic exercise, weight loss including bariatric surgery, and management of CVD risks may improve sexual function. Earlier meta-analyses reported improvement in ED with statins; the discussion of those findings does not continue in this section.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.3 Phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors
document_sections.content: The EMA has approved four selective PDE5Is for ED. Efficacy has been established across almost all ED subgroups and means obtaining rigidity sufficient for satisfying intercourse. Adverse effects are generally mild and resolve without intervention. Choose an agent with regard to intercourse frequency and the individual’s experience. Two meta-analyses favoured sildenafil 50 mg for patients prioritising efficacy and an initial tadalafil 10 mg for those prioritising tolerability. A placebo-response meta-analysis also found significant ED improvement, particularly in men with ED-related post-traumatic stress disorder. Tables 5.3 and 5.4 compare pharmacokinetics and common adverse events.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.3.1 Sildenafil
document_sections.content: Sildenafil doses are 25, 50 and 100 mg; start at 50 mg and adjust for response and adverse effects. Effectiveness begins 30-60 minutes after administration and can extend up to 12 hours. In a 24-week dose-response study, improved erections occurred in 56%, 77% and 84% of general ED patients receiving 25, 50 and 100 mg, respectively, compared with 25% on placebo. Sildenafil also significantly improved IIEF, SEP2, SEP3, GAQ and treatment-satisfaction scores. A sildenafil citrate ODT in 25, 50, 75 and 100 mg doses was developed chiefly for difficulty swallowing solid tablets; an oral suspension has also produced clinically relevant results.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.3.2 Tadalafil
document_sections.content: Tadalafil can be taken on demand at 10 or 20 mg or daily at 5 mg. Begin on-demand treatment at 10 mg and adapt to effectiveness and adverse effects. Its effect starts from 30 minutes, peaks after approximately 2 hours and can last up to 36 hours. In a 12-week study, 67% and 81% of men taking 10 and 20 mg reported improved erections, respectively, versus 35% receiving placebo. Short-term evidence also indicates a net clinical benefit for ejaculation and orgasm in patients with ED. With once-daily tadalafil 5 mg, 40% of men aged > 45 years responded for both ED and LUTS/BPH after 12 weeks. It may therefore be considered for ED alone or concomitant LUTS when one therapy is preferred.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.3.3 Vardenafil
document_sections.content: On-demand vardenafil doses are 5, 10 and 20 mg. Start at 10 mg and adjust for response and adverse effects. It works from 30 minutes after dosing; one of three patients achieved satisfactory erections within 15 minutes. In a 12-week study, improved erections occurred in 66%, 76% and 80% of men taking 5, 10 and 20 mg, respectively, versus 30% receiving placebo. IIEF, SEP2, SEP3, GAQ and treatment satisfaction improved significantly. An ODT formulation has shown efficacy in several RCTs without an apparent difference from the usual formulation.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.3.4 Avanafil
document_sections.content: Avanafil is taken on demand at 50, 100 or 200 mg. Start with 100 mg as needed 15-30 minutes before sexual activity, adjusting for effectiveness and tolerability. In a general ED population, mean percentages of successful attempts resulting in intercourse were 47%, 58% and 59% with 50, 100 and 200 mg, respectively, versus 28% with placebo. A meta-analysis found efficacy comparable to sildenafil, vardenafil and tadalafil.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.3.5 Continuous use of PDE5Is
document_sections.content: According to the EMA, tadalafil 2.5 or 5 mg once daily may be suitable according to patient preference and clinician judgement. The recommended daily dose for these patients is 5 mg at approximately the same time each day. Daily 5 mg offers an alternative to on-demand tadalafil when couples prefer spontaneous sex or expect frequent activity, without linking dosing to intercourse. Across ED populations, daily and on-demand tadalafil show no clinically significant treatment difference. Once-daily 5 mg is generally effective and well tolerated across ED severities and may improve EF after a partial response to on-demand PDE5Is. Periodically reassess whether continuous dosing remains appropriate.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.3.6 Safety concerns for PDE5Is
document_sections.content: Safety considerations include cardiovascular effects, contraindicated combinations and potential blood-pressure effects with other medicines.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.3.6.1 Cardiovascular safety
document_sections.content: RCTs and open-label studies have not demonstrated increased MI rates with PDE5Is. In an observational study of men with stable CAD, PDE5I treatment was associated with lower risks of death, MI, heart failure and revascularisation than alprostadil treatment. In stable angina, PDE5Is did not worsen total exercise duration or time to ischaemia on testing. The EAU panel maintains the 3rd Princeton Consensus Panel recommendations concerning PDE5I prescribing for patients with CVD or high cardiovascular risk.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.3.6.2 Contraindications for the concomitant use of organic nitrates and nicorandil
document_sections.content: Any concurrent organic nitrate or NO donor, including recreational amyl nitrite or nitrate, is an absolute contraindication to PDE5Is because cGMP accumulation can produce unpredictable blood-pressure falls and hypotensive symptoms. Concurrent nicorandil is also contraindicated because its nitric-oxide-donating properties can increase cGMP.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.3.6.3 Antihypertensive drugs
document_sections.content: Combining PDE5Is with antihypertensive medicines can cause small additional blood-pressure decreases, usually of minor clinical importance. Background antihypertensive treatment generally does not worsen the PDE5I adverse-event profile, including when several such agents are taken.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.3.6.4 Interactions with α-blockers
document_sections.content: Tadalafil 5 mg is the only currently licensed medicine for both ED and LUTS and has shown beneficial effects on urinary symptoms and EF. Consider tadalafil 5 mg for ED accompanying mild to moderate LUTS, alone or with α-blockers. Their shared vasodilating action warrants awareness of possible cumulative blood-pressure effects. However, a meta-analysis of combinations with non-uroselective and uro-selective α-blockers found possible haemodynamic changes without increased hypotension-related adverse events. There is currently no restriction on simultaneous use of α-blockers and PDE5I.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.3.7 Management of non- or poor-responders to PDE5Is
document_sections.content: First identify why treatment appears ineffective: verify a licensed product, appropriate prescribing and correct use. Fat-rich meals can delay absorption of sildenafil, vardenafil and avanafil; attempted intercourse may occur too soon or too long after dosing. Education about dose, timing and sexual stimulation can restore response on retrying the relevant PDE5I. Studies suggest testosterone therapy may improve PDE5I response in patients with hypogonadism; when diagnostic criteria suggest testosterone deficiency, testosterone treatment may be more appropriate even with ED. Limited data suggest switching PDE5Is could help some individuals, but available RCTs have reported no supporting evidence. Consider combination treatment as an initial approach in refractory, complex or difficult-to-treat ED, while recognising limited data. Possible combinations include PDE5Is with antioxidants, LI-SWT or VED; daily tadalafil with an on-demand short-acting PDE5I such as sildenafil; Li-SWT with VED; and PDE5Is with topical alprostadil.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.3.8 Topical/Intraurethral alprostadil
document_sections.content: Topical alprostadil cream contains a permeation enhancer and delivers 200 and 300 μg through the urethral meatus. Although clinical data remain limited, it significantly improved IIEF-EF, SEP2 and SEP3 versus placebo across mild-to-severe ED. Penile redness, burning and pain generally resolve within two hours. VITAROSTM 300 μg is available in some European countries. A randomised cross-over trial found that direct administration within the meatus improved efficacy and patient confidence without increasing adverse effects compared with standard administration. The alternative intra-urethral pellet MUSE™ contains 1251000 μg; intercourse-sufficient erections occur in 30-65.9% of patients. In practice, start at 500 μg because it is more effective than 250 μg with little difference in adverse events; increase to 1000 μg if response is inadequate. Frequent adverse events are local pain (29-41%) and dizziness with possible hypotension (1.9-14%). Fibrosis and priapism are rare (< 1%); urethral bleeding (5%) and urinary tract infections (0.2%) relate to administration. Efficacy is significantly lower than with intracavernous pharmacotherapy and long-term adherence is 30%. This route offers a less invasive but less effective alternative for patients who prefer not to use injections.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.4 Psychosocial intervention and therapy
document_sections.content: Recommended psychosocial options include sexual-skills training, marital therapy, psychosexual education and Cognitive and Behavioural Therapy (CBT - group or couple format), including online delivery. CBT targets dysfunctional thoughts and behaviours affecting ED and improves adjustment to the condition. Combining CBT with medical ED treatment has empirical support and is considered an optimal approach.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.5 Hormonal treatment
document_sections.content: When clinically indicated, intramuscular, transdermal or oral testosterone therapy can be considered for men with low or low-normal testosterone who also have reduced desire, EF difficulties and dissatisfaction with intercourse or sexual life. This consideration includes patients with a CVD history.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.6 Vacuum erection devices
document_sections.content: Reported rates of erections satisfactory for intercourse reach 90% across ED causes, while satisfaction ranges from 27% to 94%. Continued VED use falls to 50-64% after two years. Common adverse effects are pain, inability to ejaculate, petechiae, bruising and numbness. Removing the constriction ring within 30 minutes can prevent serious skin necrosis. VEDs are contraindicated with bleeding disorders or anticoagulant treatment. They may particularly suit informed older patients who have intercourse infrequently and need non-invasive, drug-free treatment because of comorbidity.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.7 Intracavernous injections therapy
document_sections.content: Intracavernous vasoactive medicines were the first medical ED therapy. In a personalised treatment plan, injections can be offered at any stage.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.7.1 Alprostadil
document_sections.content: Alprostadil (CaverjectTM, Edex/ViridalTM) is the first and only medicine approved for intracavernous ED treatment. It is the most effective monotherapy at 5-40 μg; 40 μg may be available off label in some European countries. Erection begins after 5-15 minutes, with dose-dependent but highly variable duration. Patients need office-based injection training. Efficacy exceeds 70% in general and selected diabetes or CVD populations; reported satisfaction is 87-93.5% among patients and 86-90.3% among partners. Reported complications include penile pain (50% of patients reported pain only after 11% of total injections), unwanted prolonged erection (5%), priapism (1%) and fibrosis (2%). Pain usually diminishes with continued use and may be relieved by sodium bicarbonate or local anaesthesia. Cavernosal fibrosis generally resolves within months after temporarily stopping injections; tunical fibrosis may herald Peyronie’s disease and justify permanent cessation. Systemic effects are uncommon, chiefly mild hypotension at higher doses. In a population study of 16,548 men with prior ischaemic CVD, alprostadil recipients had greater subsequent cardiovascular-event risk than PDE5I recipients. Contraindications include alprostadil hypersensitivity, risk of priapism and bleeding disorders. Intracavernous pharmacotherapy discontinuation is reported at 41-68%, mostly during the first two to three months; thorough initial counselling and close follow-up may address withdrawal.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.7.2 Other vasoactive intracavernous treatments
document_sections.content: Table 5.5 compares injection compounds. Combining agents can exploit different actions and lower individual doses and adverse effects. Papaverine 20-80 mg is usually combined with other drugs because monotherapy has frequent adverse effects; it is not licensed for ED. Phentolamine improves combination efficacy but has a poor monotherapy response and is not licensed for ED. Evidence for vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), NO donors such as linsidomine, forskolin, potassium channel openers, moxisylyte and calcitonin gene-related peptide is limited; combinations are often nonstandardised and availability varies. Bimix contains papaverine 7.5-45 mg plus phentolamine 0.25-1.5 mg. Trimix contains papaverine 8-16 mg, phentolamine 0.2-0.4 mg and alprostadil 10-20 μg. Both are widely used but unlicensed for ED. Trimix efficacy reaches 92%; adverse effects resemble alprostadil monotherapy, with less penile pain because its alprostadil dose is lower. With papaverine, fibrosis occurs more often (5-10%, depending on total dose). InvicorpTM combines vasoactive intestinal peptide 25 μg with phentolamine mesylate 1-2 mg and was effective in > 80% of men, including prior treatment nonresponders, with little penile pain and virtually negligible priapism risk. Despite high combination efficacy, 5-10% of patients do not respond.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.8 Innovative treatment modalities
document_sections.content: Several possible new ED treatments are being studied. Most require larger blinded, placebo-controlled randomised trials before evidence-based, clinically reliable recommendation grades can be assigned.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.8.1 Regenerative medicine therapies
document_sections.content: The following sections discuss shockwave treatment, platelet-rich plasma and stem-cell approaches.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.8.1.1 Shockwave therapy
document_sections.content: LI-SWT has increasingly been proposed for vasculogenic ED and is the only currently marketed treatment described as potentially curative. Single-arm trials generally show improvement in patient-reported EF, but generators, focal versus radial waves, settings, protocols and outcomes vary considerably. One parameter trial found no significant differences between energy-flux levels, although 0.10 mJ/mm2 appeared slightly better than lower levels. Most trials used focal generators; an RCT of radial waves found no IIEF-EF or EHS difference versus placebo. Most studies suggest significant but modest IIEF and EHS gains in mild vasculogenic ED, with satisfactory improvement reported by 40-80%. A few studies reported better penile haemodynamics, of uncertain clinical meaning. LI-SWT may also improve erections in severe ED with absent or inadequate PDE5I response, potentially delaying more invasive treatment. Effects become clinically evident from one to three months after treatment, then progressively decline, although some may remain detectable up to five years. RCTs suggest combination with VED in men with T2DM or with daily tadalafil could improve outcomes. A recent meta-analysis found a positive effect of LI-ESWT on early EF recovery during rehabilitation after RP, but its authors considered the evidence low quality and urged cautious interpretation.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.8.1.2 Platelet-Rich Plasma
document_sections.content: Prospective and retrospective studies have examined intracavernous PRP. Its proposed regenerative action involves concentrated platelets containing VEGF, EGF, IGF-1, PDGF and FGF, potentially stimulating angiogenesis and stem-cell recruitment. In an RCT, 60 men with mild to moderate vasculogenic ED received two 10 mL injections of PRP (n = 30) or placebo (n = 30). At 1, 3 and 6-month follow-up, significantly more PRP recipients reached an IIEF-EF minimal clinically important difference (MCID); at 6 months, rates were 69% versus 27% (p < 0.001). Mean IIEF-EF improvement was 2.7 points at 1-month and 3.9 points at 6-month after treatment. No bleeding events or other adverse effects were reported. A double-blind placebo-controlled randomised study of 109 patients aged 45-65 years with mild to moderate ED found significantly better IIEF-EF, SEP2 and SEP3 after PRP at 1, 3 and 6 months; MCID at 6-month was reached by 70% versus 16%. Another small double-blind placebo-controlled randomised study using two PRP injections 1 month apart found treatment safe but no efficacy difference; participants could continue PDE5Is. A meta-analysis of these RCTs found a mean IIEF-EF improvement with PRP versus placebo of 3.21 [95%CI: 1.82; 4.60] at 6 months. Despite encouraging results in primary organic ED, evidence remains insufficient for a clinical-practice recommendation. Timing, dosing, activation, platelet concentration and growth-factor or cytokine composition remain unresolved. Intracavernous PRP should therefore be used only within clinical trials pending larger efficacy and safety studies.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.8.1.3 Stem-cells
document_sections.content: Stem-cell treatment for ED remains investigational. A systematic review of 18 phase I and II trials involving 373 patients found substantial variation in cell types, protocols and patient characteristics. Intracavernous injection appeared safe, but efficacy cannot be established because only four small trials had placebo controls and their results conflicted. Evidence remains insufficient for a clinical recommendation.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.8.2 Botulinum Neurotoxin
document_sections.content: Botulinum Neurotoxin A (BoNT-A) has been investigated for ED unresponsive to PDE5Is or intracavernous pro-erectile drugs. In one RCT, 70 PDE5I-refractory patients received one intracavernous injection of BoNT-A 100 UI or saline while continuing high-dose on-demand PDE5Is. EHS and PSV improved at two weeks; at six weeks SHIM improved by 5 points with BoNT-A versus no improvement with placebo, and 53% reported an erection firm enough for vaginal penetration. A second RCT randomised 176 patients unresponsive to PDE5Is or ICI trimix to BoNT-A 100 UI, BoNT-A 50 UI or placebo. Both active groups showed significant SHIM, EHS and SEP improvement, with peak response at three months; up to 40% resumed satisfactory sexual activity. Both trials reported only mild local effects and no systemic complications. Uncontrolled studies also reported promising findings, but larger studies are required to establish efficacy and safety; no clinical-practice recommendation can currently be made.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.9 Herbal medicine and natural supplements
document_sections.content: Use of herbal products and supplements for ED has expanded despite little robust evidence of efficacy or safety. A Cochrane review found that ginseng may offer only trivial benefit for EF or intercourse satisfaction versus placebo on validated measures. A meta-analysis of 18 antioxidant trials found L-arginine increased IIEF-EF by a mean of 2.74 (95%CI 1.67,3.81) compared with placebo, a small but significant effect, without improving sexual-satisfaction scores. Similar findings were reported for folic acid, myoinositol, vitamin-E, L-carnitine, nicotinic acid, pine bark extract, transresveratrol, L-citrulline and ginseng; patients may not perceive such small changes as meaningful. Another meta-analysis linked PDE5Is plus antioxidants, including propionyl-L-carnitine, acetyl-L-carnitine, L-arginine, folic acid and trans-resveratrol, to greater EF improvement than PDE5Is alone. Overall, these products alone or with PDE5Is might offer a small benefit, but its clinical significance requires further study.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.10 Erectile dysfunction after radical prostatectomy
document_sections.content: Urologists should proactively discuss and offer care for ED and other sexual problems after RP. Pro-erectile medicines help postoperative EF and resumption of sexual activity. Trials have shown EF improvement with therapeutic or prophylactic ED medicines after RP. Early rather than delayed EF treatment affects natural recovery time, but data are limited for identifying an optimal rehabilitation regimen or achieving spontaneous unassisted erections. A small pilot RCT suggested perioperative PDE5I rehabilitation may improve recovery compared with postoperative initiation. Nonetheless, there is no evidence that penile rehabilitation itself increases spontaneous EF recovery after nerve-sparing RP (NSRP). PDE5Is are regarded as first-line after nerve-sparing surgery regardless of operative technique; age, baseline EF and nerve-sparing quality predict outcomes. In a Cochrane review of eight RCTs, scheduled PDE5Is may have little or no effect on self-reported potency up to 12 months compared with placebo or no treatment, and daily use made little to no difference to short- or long-term EF. Its authors found no improvement over on-demand PDE5Is for self-reported EF. Conversely, a meta-analysis of 22 trials and 16 rehabilitation protocols ranked daily sildenafil 100 mg as most effective for EF recovery. Intracavernous injections and implants have been proposed as second- and third-line options when oral PDE5Is are ineffective or unsuitable. A meta-analysis reported strong therapeutic effects and no serious adverse events with early VED use, supporting consideration as an alternative. Two network meta-analyses favoured VED plus PDE5is over monotherapy, supporting consideration of the combination. A penile traction device preserved penile length better than no treatment in one study. A systematic review considered PFMT with bio-feedback promising, but called for adequately powered, rigorous RCTs before firm conclusions.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.11 Surgical management
document_sections.content: Surgical options discussed include selected post-traumatic arterial revascularisation and penile prosthesis implantation; venous ligation is not recommended.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.11.1 Surgery for post-traumatic arteriogenic ED
document_sections.content: For young patients following pelvic or perineal trauma, penile revascularisation has reported long-term success of 60-70%. Confirm stenosis with penile pharmaco-arteriography. Corporeal veno-occlusive dysfunction contraindicates revascularisation and must be excluded using dynamic infusion cavernosometry or cavernosography.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.11.2 Venous ligation surgery
document_sections.content: Venous ligation for veno-occlusive dysfunction is no longer recommended because long-term outcomes are poor.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.11.2.1 Penile prostheses
document_sections.content: Consider implantation for patients unsuitable for pharmacotherapies or preferring definitive treatment, and for those unresponsive to other options. Available classes are inflatable two- or three-piece devices and semi-rigid malleable, mechanical or soft flexible devices. No direct manufacturer comparisons establish one implant type as superior. A three-piece inflatable device may be preferred for a more natural erection, but prospective RCTs have not compared satisfaction across implant types. A two-piece implant may suit patients at high risk from reservoir placement, including those with prior abdominal surgery. Semi-rigid implants are simpler to place and use and may suit limited hand dexterity, but remain persistently firm and may be harder to conceal. Peno-scrotal and infrapubic implantation approaches have no demonstrated overall advantage over one another; surgeons are advised to know both and tailor the incision in complex cases. With appropriate counselling, patient satisfaction is 92-100% and partner satisfaction 91-95%. Targeted psychosexual counselling may improve sexuality and well-being after implantation. Evidence supports recommending implantation when less invasive therapies fail because of efficacy, safety and satisfaction. Major complications are mechanical failure and infection. Technical improvements have produced failure rates of < 5% after 5 years for commonly used three-piece devices. A meta-analysis estimated implant survival at 93.3% at 1 year, 91.0% at 3 years, 87.2% at 5 years, 76.8% at 10 years, 63.7% at 15 years and 52.9% at 20 years. Careful technique and prophylaxis covering Gram-positive and negative bacteria reduced primary-implant infection to 2-3% in low-risk patients at high-volume centres; antibiotic-impregnated or hydrophilic-coated implants may lower it further to 1-2%. Coated implants, reduced wound exposure and minimal skin contact appear helpful. Evidence remains inconclusive for prolonged postoperative antibiotics (> 24 hours), clipper shaving and chlorhexidine-alcohol preparation. In an RCT, identifying and treating nasal Staphylococcus aureus carriage with mupirocin and chlorhexidine before surgery reduced surgical-site infection from 4.4% to 0.9%. Database evidence associates diabetes mellitus and, independently, hypogonadism with implant infection. No RCT establishes an acceptable preoperative glycated-haemoglobin threshold for patients with diabetes. A retrospective multicentre diabetes cohort receiving Coloplast Titan™ implants found vancomycin plus gentamicin the most effective dipping-antibiotic combination for preventing infection, explantation and revision. Published spinal-cord-injury series report prosthesis infection in up to 16%. Infection requires device removal and antibiotics; immediate wash-out, salvage and replacement have achieved > 80% success in reported series. No absolute choice between explantation alone and salvage can be given without discussing both approaches with the patient. Erosion of distal corpora, urethra or glans occurs in 1-6%; reservoir-related damage to bladder, bowel or vessels can occur, and glans ischaemia or necrosis has been reported in about 1.5%. Serious-complication risk is higher with substantial vascular impairment, including diabetes, or concurrent penile-lengthening procedures.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.12 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of ED
document_sections.content: The evidence summary rates lifestyle-related ED improvement in selected populations, PDE5I-associated EF improvement and safety, lack of demonstrated efficacy differences between PDE5Is, effective but frequently discontinued intracavernous alprostadil, modest LI-SWT benefit in vasculogenic ED, and lack of increased spontaneous EF recovery from PDE5I rehabilitation after RP as LE 1a. It rates effective but still insufficiently studied topical or intra-urethral alprostadil, preliminary PRP-related improvement with insufficient evidence for a recommendation, and preliminary BoNT-A response improvement with limited data as LE 1b. VED-associated EF improvement with variable satisfaction is LE 2b. Absence of demonstrated differences between implant types or surgical approaches in efficacy and safety is LE 3. Strong: explain PDE5I action and correct administration fully, because misuse and inadequate information are major reasons for apparent nonresponse. Strong: refer for Cognitive Behaviour Therapy, involving the partner where appropriate and combining it with medical care when indicated. Strong: discuss sexual changes beyond ED with patients receiving active PCa treatment, including reduced desire, altered orgasm, anejaculation, Peyronie’s-like disease and penile-size changes. Strong: begin lifestyle and risk-factor modification before or alongside ED treatment. Strong: use PDE5Is first line. Strong: offer intracavernous injections as an alternative first-line choice for informed patients or as second-line therapy. Weak: offer topical or intra-urethral alprostadil as an alternative first-line option to informed patients who cannot or do not want oral vasoactive treatment, do not want injections, or prefer a less invasive approach. Weak: use LI-SWT with or without PDE5Is for mild vasculogenic ED, as an informed alternative when oral vasoactive drugs are unsuitable or unwanted, or for vasculogenic ED with poor PDE5I response. Weak: offer VEDs to informed patients seeking drug-free, non-invasive management. Weak: after counselling that EF gains may be mild, use daily L-arginine or ginseng supplements for mild ED when pharmacological treatment is refused. Strong: implant a penile prosthesis after other treatments fail or according to patient preference, following full discussion of benefits and harms. Weak: explain that evidence does not support any particular penile-rehabilitation regimen. Weak: start pro-erectile treatment as early as possible after RP, pelvic surgery or other curative PCa treatment.

document_sections.heading: 5.7 Follow-up
document_sections.content: Follow-up should assess treatment effectiveness, safety and patient satisfaction; successful ED care is not determined by efficacy and safety alone. No single treatment suits every patient or every circumstance.
